lessons.title: What a project is, and what a project manager does
lessons.subtitle: Most work is not a project. Learn the difference, because it changes how you plan, lead and measure success.
outcomes: Tell a project apart from ongoing work using three clear tests
Explain scope, time, cost and quality as linked limits
Describe what a project manager is actually responsible for
lessons.body:
Adaeze runs the front desk of a small clinic in Enugu. For three years her job has been the same each day: greet patients, book appointments, file records. Then the owner says, "We are moving to a new building in four months, and I want you to handle it." Nobody trains her. Nobody tells her where to start. She opens her notebook and writes "move clinic" at the top of a blank page. That is where most people meet project management: handed a big job with a date on it and no method. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

This course is the method. By the end you will be able to take a job like Adaeze's, break it into pieces, put dates and people on it, watch for trouble, and finish. This first lesson gives you the base: what counts as a project, what makes it hard, and what the person in charge is really there to do.

## A project has an end, and it makes something new

The Project Management Institute (PMI), the largest professional body in the field, describes a project as a temporary effort to create a unique product, service or result. Three words matter.

- **Temporary.** It has a start and an end. When the result is delivered, the project is over, even if what it made lasts for years.
- **Unique.** The result is not a copy of last time. Even if you have moved offices before, this building, this staff and this budget are different.
- **Result.** Something exists at the end that did not exist at the start: a new branch, a working website, a finished wedding, a trained team.

Compare that with **operations**, the work that repeats. Booking patients is operations. Cooking at a restaurant every evening is operations. Running payroll every month is operations. Operations aim to do the same thing reliably and efficiently. Projects aim to change something once.

:::figure
type: versus
title: Project or ongoing work?
caption: A project is temporary and creates something new, while ongoing work repeats the same process again and again. Most real jobs mix the two.
left: Project
right: Ongoing work
- Time | Has a start and a finish | Continues with no planned end
- Result | Something new and unique | The same output each cycle
- Main aim | Deliver the change on time and within limits | Keep it steady and efficient
- Example | Opening a second pharmacy branch | Serving customers at the first branch every day
:::

Why does the difference matter? Because the two need different habits. In operations you improve a process that already works. In a project there is no process yet. You are designing it as you go, with a deadline, so you need planning, estimating and risk checks that a repeating job rarely needs.

:::check q1-1
:::

## Why projects are hard

A repeating job has a long history of data. A project does not, and that creates three standing problems.

1. **Uncertainty.** You are estimating work you have not done before. Some of your guesses will be wrong.
2. **Dependencies.** Task B cannot start until task A finishes, and task A belongs to someone else.
3. **Competing wishes.** The owner wants it cheap, the staff want it comfortable, the landlord wants it Tuesday.

The numbers back up how common trouble is. Bent Flyvbjerg, an emeritus professor at Oxford, built a database of about 16,000 projects across many fields. He reports that only about 8.5 percent met their original cost and time estimates. Keep in mind that his data leans toward large projects such as infrastructure and technology, so do not read it as a rule for a school fundraiser. But the lesson holds at every size: finishing exactly as first planned is the exception. Good project management does not promise zero surprises. It builds the habits that find surprises early and reduce their cost.

## The four limits: scope, time, cost, quality

Every project lives inside limits that pull against each other. Most textbooks start with three, often drawn as a triangle: **scope** (what you will deliver), **time** (when), and **cost** (how much money and effort). A fourth, **quality** (how well it must work), sits in the middle, because squeezing any of the three usually damages it.

The useful insight is that they are linked. Change one and at least one other must move.

- Add more to the scope, and either the date moves or the cost rises.
- Cut the deadline, and you must cut scope or add money.
- Cut the budget, and you must cut scope or accept a later date, or both.

Adaeze's owner says, "Same budget, same quality, and open in three months instead of four." A good project manager does not just say "we will try." She says, "To gain a month we must pick one: spend more on movers working extra shifts, or leave the second waiting room unfinished. Which do you want?" You will use this move again and again: make the trade-off visible and let the decision-maker choose.

:::example title=The trade-off conversation (invented numbers)
A school in Abuja plans a science fair. The plan: 30 student stalls, a hall hired for two days, budget of ₦900,000, date fixed for 14 March.

In February the head teacher asks to add a third day for parents who work during the week. The project manager, a teacher called Mr Okoro, works out what that does:

- Hall hire for a third day: ₦150,000 extra.
- Supervising teachers for one more day: ₦60,000 extra in allowances.
- Total new cost: ₦900,000 + ₦150,000 + ₦60,000 = ₦1,110,000.

He goes back with three options instead of a complaint:

1. Keep three days and raise the budget to ₦1,110,000.
2. Keep three days inside ₦900,000 by cutting the stalls from 30 to 15, which saves the ₦210,000 needed in stall materials, prizes and extra helpers.
3. Stay at two days and add an evening session on day two for working parents, at about ₦40,000 for extra lighting and security.

The head teacher picks option 3. Notice what Mr Okoro did. He did not say yes, and he did not say no. He showed the effect on scope, time and cost, and the owner of the decision decided.
:::

## What a project manager actually does

A project manager is not the person who does the most work, or who knows the most about the subject. The job is to make sure the right work happens, in the right order, by the right people, and that problems surface while they are still small. In practice that breaks into six areas, and this course follows them:

1. **Define** what success looks like and what is out of bounds (Module 1).
2. **Plan** the work, the time, the money and the risks (Module 2).
3. **Lead** the people, so they know what to do and why (Module 3).
4. **Track** progress against the plan and react early (Module 3).
5. **Communicate** with everyone who cares about the result, in the way they need (Modules 1 and 3).
6. **Close** the project properly, hand over the result and learn from it (Module 4).

You do not need a title to do this. If you have ever organised a family event, a church programme or a school trip, you have done a version of it. A professional approach simply makes the work repeatable, so you are not relying on luck and late nights.

:::keyidea
A project is temporary work that creates something new, and the manager's job is to deliver it inside linked limits of scope, time, cost and quality by making trade-offs visible early.
:::

## Success is more than "done on time"

One more idea before you start. A project can arrive on the date and on budget and still fail, if what it delivered does not solve the real problem. A clinic that moves on schedule but cannot get patients through the new door has not succeeded. So success has two parts: **delivery success** (did we finish within the agreed limits?) and **result success** (does what we made actually work for the people who need it?). Lesson 3 will show you how to write both down before work begins.

## What you can do now

You can tell a project from ongoing work, name the four limits, explain a trade-off to someone who wants everything, and describe the six areas of a project manager's job. In Lesson 2 you will learn the main ways projects are run, from step-by-step plans to short repeating cycles, and how to choose between them.

:::exercise title=Spot the project
1. Write down five pieces of work you or people around you did in the last month. Mix big and small: for example, a wedding, cooking daily meals, a phone repair, a shop restock, a job application.
2. For each, apply the three tests: Does it have a planned end? Is the result new or unique? Does something exist at the end that did not exist before? Mark each one "project", "operations" or "mixed".
3. Pick one real project from your list, or one coming up. Write one sentence for each limit: what is the scope, the date, the budget, and the quality bar?
4. Now answer this: if someone asked you to finish a month earlier, which of the other limits would you change first, and why?

A good answer ends with a sentence of the form "If the date moves earlier, I would change ___ because ___."
:::

lessons.title: Life cycles and methods: plan-first, agile and hybrid
lessons.subtitle: Every project passes through the same stages, but there is more than one way to run them. Learn to choose.
outcomes: Name the stages every project passes through
Compare plan-first (predictive) and agile approaches and say when each fits
Choose a method for a real project using four questions
lessons.body:
Two cousins both get projects in the same week. Ngozi is building a three-bedroom house in Ibadan. Tunde is building a mobile app for a bakery. Ngozi's contractor draws full plans, gets them approved, orders materials and builds in a fixed order. Tunde's team builds a rough version of the ordering screen in a week, shows it to the baker, and changes it based on what she says. Both are doing good project management. Neither could swap methods without trouble. You cannot change the foundation of a house after the roof is on, and you cannot know what a baker wants in an app until she tries one. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

This lesson gives you the map: the stages every project passes through, the main families of method, and a practical way to choose.

## The stages every project passes through

Whatever method you use, the work moves through the same broad stages. Different books use slightly different names, but the shape is stable.

:::figure
type: flow
title: The project life cycle
caption: Five stages in order, from starting the project to closing it. Monitoring and controlling runs alongside planning and doing, not after them.
- Initiate | Why are we doing this, and who is in charge?
- Plan | What, who, when, how much, what could go wrong?
- Execute | Do the work and lead the team
- Monitor | Compare progress with the plan and correct
- Close | Hand over, review, release the team
:::

In plain words:

- **Initiate.** Decide the project is worth doing and give someone the authority to run it. You write a short document, often called a **project charter**, that names the purpose, the manager and the main limits. Lesson 3 covers this.
- **Plan.** Work out the scope, schedule, budget, people, risks and how you will communicate. Module 2 covers this.
- **Execute.** The team does the work. The manager leads, removes obstacles and keeps people informed.
- **Monitor and control.** While work happens, you check actual progress against the plan, spot differences and decide what to do. This is not a final stage. It runs the whole time.
- **Close.** Confirm the result is accepted, hand it over, settle the accounts, record what you learned and let the team go.

Beginners tend to skip two stages: the thinking at the start ("is this the right project, and what does success mean?") and the closing at the end ("did it work, and what do we do differently next time?"). Those two are where a large share of avoidable failure begins and where a large share of learning is lost.

## Plan-first projects (predictive)

In a **predictive** approach, you do most of the planning up front, then execute the plan, and manage changes through a formal process. People often call it "waterfall" because work flows down through stages: requirements, design, build, test, deliver.

It works best when:

- The result is clear before you start (a building, a road, an event, a product that must meet a legal standard).
- Changes are expensive once work has started. Moving a wall after the concrete has set costs real money.
- Different parties need fixed dates and prices to sign contracts.

Its weakness is that if your early assumptions were wrong, you may find out late, when changing is costly.

## Agile projects (iterative and adaptive)

An **agile** approach plans in short cycles. You build a small, usable piece, show it to the people who will use it, learn from their reaction, and decide what to build next. Teams often work in cycles of one to four weeks.

Agile grew mostly out of software teams who found that big up-front plans kept going out of date. In 2001 a group of seventeen practitioners wrote the *Manifesto for Agile Software Development*. It states four value pairs and then adds that there is value in the items on the right, but the items on the left are valued more:

- Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
- Working software over comprehensive documentation
- Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
- Responding to change over following a plan

Read that carefully. It does not say "no plans" or "no documents". It says that when they conflict, people and working results come first.

It works best when:

- You cannot know the full requirements at the start, because users will only know what they want when they see something.
- Change is cheap, as in software, content, marketing campaigns and design work.
- You can get frequent feedback from real users.

Its weakness is that without discipline it can drift. If nobody is clear about the goal, a team can deliver many small pieces that never add up to what the sponsor wanted. Agile also fits badly when a fixed price and exact date are demanded in a contract before anything is known.

## Hybrid: using both

Real projects are often a mix. A hospital building is predictive in its structure, but the layout of the waiting area may be tested with staff on paper models first. A software launch can be agile in how the product is built, but predictive in its marketing calendar and budget approvals. A **hybrid** approach simply uses each style where it fits. There is nothing impure about it. The aim is the result, not loyalty to a label.

:::figure
type: versus
title: Predictive and agile at a glance
caption: Predictive plans most of the work first and manages change formally. Agile plans a little at a time and expects the plan to change as people learn.
left: Predictive
right: Agile
- Planning | Mostly done before work starts | Done in short rounds, again and again
- Change | Handled through a formal request | Expected and welcomed
- Delivery | Result arrives near the end | Usable pieces arrive regularly
- Best when | Requirements are clear and change is costly | Requirements are unclear and change is cheap
:::

:::check q2-1
:::

## Frameworks you will hear about

You will meet names. A one-line orientation helps:

- **PMBOK Guide**, from PMI: a body of knowledge describing good practice across many project types. It is a reference, not a step-by-step recipe.
- **PRINCE2**: a structured method widely used in the UK and in many public-sector projects around the world. Its seven principles include continued business justification and learning from experience.
- **Scrum**: a lightweight agile framework built on short cycles called Sprints. Lesson 11 covers it.
- **Kanban**: a way of visualising work on a board and limiting how much is in progress at once. Lesson 11 covers it too.

You do not need to pick one religion. They share more than they differ: clear goals, visible work, regular checking, and learning.

## Four questions to choose a method

Ask these at the start of any project.

1. **How clear is the result?** Clear and stable points toward predictive. Fuzzy points toward agile.
2. **What does a change cost once work has started?** High cost points toward predictive. Low cost points toward agile.
3. **Can I get feedback often from real users?** Yes points toward agile. No makes agile much harder.
4. **Do contracts or regulations demand fixed scope, price or date?** Yes pushes toward predictive, at least for the outer shell.

:::example title=Choosing for three projects (invented scenarios)
**A. A church building a 400-seat auditorium.** The design is fixed by an architect and local approvals. Concrete, steel and roofing must happen in order. Changes are costly. Answers: clear, costly to change, little user feedback possible mid-build, regulations apply. **Predictive.**

**B. A student group building a free study-planner website.** Nobody knows which features students will actually use. A change to the design costs a few hours. The team can show the site to classmates every week. **Agile**, in two-week cycles.

**C. A company launching a new soap product.** The factory setup, packaging order and launch date are fixed by contracts. But the advertising messages can be tested with small groups and adjusted. **Hybrid**: a predictive plan for factory and supply, agile cycles for the marketing.

Notice the method was chosen by looking at the project, not at what the manager likes best.
:::

:::compare
weak: "We are an agile team, so we do not need a plan or a budget."
strong: "We work in two-week cycles, and we still have a goal, a budget limit and a date the sponsor can rely on. Inside those, the plan adapts."
note: Agile changes how you plan, not whether you plan.
:::

:::keyidea
Choose the method from the project's facts, meaning how clear the result is, what change costs and how often you can get feedback, and do not choose it from habit or fashion.
:::

## What you can do now

You can name the five stages, explain predictive and agile in a sentence each, say what hybrid means, and run the four-question test on a project. In Lesson 3 you will start a project properly: defining the goal, the scope and what success looks like in writing.

:::exercise title=Pick a method and defend it
1. Choose one real project, current or imagined: a small shop renovation, a community clean-up, a school app, a product launch, a wedding.
2. Answer the four questions in one line each.
3. Decide: predictive, agile or hybrid. If hybrid, say which parts use which approach.
4. Write two sentences that you could say to a sponsor to explain your choice without jargon.
5. Finally, name one risk that comes with your choice and what you would do about it. For example, predictive risks late discovery of wrong assumptions, so you might test one small piece early.

A good answer shows a clear link between your four answers and your decision.
:::

lessons.title: Start right: goals, scope and the project charter
lessons.subtitle: A project that starts with a vague goal usually ends with an argument. Write the goal, the boundaries and the proof of success on one page.
outcomes: Turn a vague wish into a clear goal with measurable success criteria
Write a scope statement that says what is in and what is out
Draft a one-page project charter
lessons.body:
Remember Adaeze and the clinic move? Suppose the owner's first instruction is, "Just make the move go smoothly." Four months later the clinic is in the new building. The owner is unhappy because the pharmacy shelves are not fitted. The nurses are unhappy because nobody told them they were expected to pack their own rooms. Adaeze is unhappy because she thought "smoothly" meant "no patient misses an appointment", and that is not what happened either. Everyone worked hard. Everyone had a different picture in their head. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

Most project arguments are not about work. They are about expectations that were never written down. Fixing that is the cheapest, most valuable thing a project manager does, and it takes about one hour at the start.

## Start with why

Before you plan anything, find out the reason. A project exists to solve a problem or to take a chance. Ask the sponsor, the person who is paying or who has the authority to approve it:

- What is wrong now, or what opportunity are we chasing?
- What will be different if this project succeeds?
- What happens if we do nothing?

For the clinic: "Our current building has a lease ending in four months, the rent is rising, and we have outgrown the space, which limits us to about 25 patients a day." That is a reason. It tells you the date is real, money matters, and the new space should hold more patients. "Move smoothly" tells you none of that.

## Turn the wish into a goal you can check

A good goal can be checked by someone who was not in the room. A well-known memory aid is **SMART**. A common modern version is specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound. It is usually credited to George T. Doran, who published an early form in a 1981 management article using slightly different words (assignable, realistic and time-related). Later writers have changed the words again, so you will see several versions. Do not argue about the letters. Use the idea: a goal should be clear, countable, possible, worth doing and dated.

:::compare
weak: Make the clinic move go smoothly.
strong: Open the new clinic at 12 Market Road on 1 March, with all five consulting rooms working, no more than one day of lost appointments, and the move completed within a ₦3,500,000 budget.
note: The strong goal can be checked by anyone. Either the rooms work on 1 March or they do not. (Invented numbers, for practice.)
:::

If you cannot measure the goal directly, find a close signal. "Better customer service" is hard to count. "Replies to WhatsApp enquiries within one hour during opening hours" can be counted from message timestamps.

:::check q3-1
:::

## Scope: what is in and what is out

**Scope** is the full list of what the project will deliver. A **scope statement** describes it in words. Its most important feature is not what it includes. It is what it explicitly excludes. Without exclusions, people assume what they want is included.

Write three lists:

1. **In scope.** What you will deliver. "Packing, moving and setting up the five consulting rooms, the reception and the records room."
2. **Out of scope.** What you will not deliver. "Buying new medical equipment. Renovating the building. Changing the clinic's computer system."
3. **Not decided yet.** Questions you must answer before the plan is firm. "Who pays for the new signboard?"

Out-of-scope items are not failures. They are protection. When someone asks in month three, "Can we also repaint the waiting room?", you can point to the page and say, "That was outside the scope we agreed. We can add it, and here is what it would cost and how it would move the date." That sentence is the foundation of **scope control**, which you will use in Lesson 13.

## Success criteria: how we will know

Write down the tests the result must pass before the sponsor accepts it. These are **acceptance criteria** or **success criteria**. Include both kinds from Lesson 1:

- **Delivery criteria:** on or before 1 March, within ₦3,500,000.
- **Result criteria:** every consulting room has working power, water and a patient bed; the records are complete and findable; the first week of appointments runs without a patient turned away because of the move.

If you agree on these early, the final handover is a simple check against the list, not a debate.

## Assumptions, constraints and the first look at risk

Three more short lists make a plan honest.

- **Constraints** are limits you cannot change: the lease ends on 28 February, the budget is capped, the building has only one lift.
- **Assumptions** are things you are treating as true without proof: "The landlord will allow access to the new building from 10 February." Each assumption is a possible risk. If it turns out false, the plan shifts.
- **Known risks** are things that could go wrong. You will develop this fully in Lesson 9, but even a quick list of three or four at the start helps.

## The project charter

All of the above fits on one page called the **project charter**. A charter is a short document that formally starts the project. It records why the project exists, who is in charge, and what the main limits are. The sponsor signs it, or at minimum agrees to it in writing, for example by email or a WhatsApp message saved in the project folder. That agreement gives the manager authority to use resources and make decisions, and gives everyone a document to return to when memories differ.

A practical charter has these parts:

| Part | What it says |
|---|---|
| Purpose | The problem or opportunity, in two sentences |
| Goal and success criteria | Measurable, with dates |
| Scope | In, out, not decided yet |
| Key dates | Start, finish, and one or two fixed milestones |
| Budget | The ceiling and where it comes from |
| People | Sponsor, project manager, main team members |
| Assumptions and constraints | The short lists above |
| First risks | Three or four |

:::example title=A one-page charter (invented project)
**Project:** Move Greenfield Clinic to 12 Market Road.

**Purpose:** The current lease ends on 28 February and the space limits us to about 25 patients a day. The new building has five consulting rooms and room for 40 patients a day.

**Goal and success criteria:** Open on 1 March with all five consulting rooms working. No more than one day of lost appointments. Move completed within ₦3,500,000. Patient records complete and findable on day one.

**In scope:** packing, transport, setting up rooms, reception and records room, informing patients. **Out of scope:** new equipment, renovation, IT system change. **Not decided:** who pays for the signboard.

**Key dates:** building access from 10 February; move weekend 22 to 23 February; opening 1 March.

**People:** Sponsor: Dr Eze (owner). Project manager: Adaeze. Team: two nurses, one cleaner, a hired transport company.

**Assumptions:** the landlord allows access from 10 February; the transport company is available on 22 and 23 February. **Constraints:** lease ends 28 February; one lift in the new building.

**First risks:** transport company cancels; power connection delayed; records lost or mixed in transit.

Sponsor agreement: Dr Eze replied "Agreed, go ahead" by email on the date the charter was sent.
:::

:::keyidea
Before planning, write the goal, scope with exclusions, and success criteria on one page the sponsor has agreed to, because most project arguments come from expectations nobody wrote down.
:::

## Common mistakes

- **Starting without a sponsor.** If no one has the authority to say yes, you will not get decisions or money.
- **Treating the charter as paperwork.** If you write it only to satisfy a rule, nobody reads it, and it fails to prevent arguments. Keep it short enough to be read.
- **Writing goals as activities.** "Hold meetings with suppliers" is an activity. "Three supplier contracts signed by 30 March" is a goal.
- **Skipping exclusions.** The out-of-scope list is the part people most often leave out and later most often need.

## What you can do now

You can find the reason behind a project, write a goal that someone else could check, write a scope statement with exclusions, list success criteria, and combine them into a one-page charter. In Lesson 4 you will find out who else cares about the project, because the people around it decide more about its success than any schedule.

:::exercise title=Write a one-page charter
1. Take a real project you are about to do or could do: organising an event, starting a small side business, a house move, a group project, a community drive.
2. Fill in every row of the charter table from this lesson. Keep it on one page, about 200 to 300 words.
3. Make sure the goal contains at least one number and one date.
4. Write at least three out-of-scope items.
5. Send it to one person who would be affected, such as a co-organiser or a family member, and ask them to answer one question: "What is missing or unclear?" Note what they say and update the charter.

A good result is a charter that the other person could read and then explain back to you in their own words.
:::

lessons.title: Stakeholders and the communication plan
lessons.subtitle: Projects succeed or fail through people. Learn to find everyone who matters, understand what they want, and keep them informed without drowning them.
outcomes: Identify stakeholders and sort them by power and interest
Choose a different approach for each group
Write a simple communication plan
lessons.body:
A women's cooperative in Kano builds a new market stall block. The plan is excellent: drawings approved, materials ordered, builders booked. Two weeks into construction, work stops. The local traders' association was never told, and its chairman says the block blocks the path their goods trucks use. Nobody was lazy. Nobody was wrong about the drawings. The project simply never asked, "Who else cares about this, and what do they need?" *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

A **stakeholder** is anyone who can affect your project or be affected by it. That includes people who help, people who pay, people who use the result, and people who will be annoyed by it. The second group, the people who might block you, are often the ones who are forgotten.

## Step 1: List everyone

Sit with a blank page and ask five questions. Who pays? Who approves? Who does the work? Who will use the result? Who could be disturbed or harmed by it? Add anyone who can stop you: a regulator, a landlord, a union, a neighbour, a community leader.

For the Kano stall block, the list might include the cooperative members, the funder, the builders, the material suppliers, the local government office that issues permits, the traders' association, the neighbouring shop owners, and the customers who will use the market. The traders' association is on that list because the question "who could be disturbed?" would have caught it.

Do this early, and repeat it. New stakeholders appear as the project moves.

## Step 2: Understand each one

For each stakeholder, write three short notes.

- **What do they want?** Their goal, fear or interest. Not what you wish they wanted.
- **How much influence do they have?** Can they stop, delay, fund or approve the project?
- **How do they feel about it right now?** Supportive, neutral, or against?

You will not always know. Where you do not, write "ask". The best way to find out is to talk to them. Fifteen minutes with a person early costs much less than a project stop later.

## Step 3: Sort them by power and interest

A simple and widely used tool is the **power and interest grid**, often credited to Aubrey Mendelow. You place each stakeholder on two lines: how much **power** they have over the project, and how much **interest** they have in it. That gives four boxes and four approaches.

:::figure
type: matrix
title: Power and interest grid
caption: Stakeholders are sorted by how much power they hold and how interested they are. High power with high interest means manage closely, high power with low interest means keep satisfied, low power with high interest means keep informed, and low on both means monitor.
x: Interest | Low interest | High interest
y: Power | Low power | High power
tl: Keep satisfied | Do not overload them, but never surprise them
tr: Manage closely | Involve them early and often
bl: Monitor | Light touch, watch for change
br: Keep informed | Regular updates, welcome their input
hot: tr
:::

How to use each box:

- **Manage closely (high power, high interest).** The sponsor, the main funder, the key customer. Talk often. Involve them in decisions. Never let them hear bad news from someone else.
- **Keep satisfied (high power, lower interest).** A regulator, a senior executive with many other concerns. Do not send long reports they will not read, but make sure they get the short version they need and that nothing surprises them.
- **Keep informed (low power, high interest).** Team members, users, neighbours. They care a lot and can raise problems you would miss. Give regular, honest updates and listen to what they say.
- **Monitor (low power, low interest).** Check now and then. People move between boxes, and today's quiet observer can become tomorrow's objector.

:::check q4-1
:::

:::example title=The Kano market stalls, redone (invented scenario)
After the stoppage, the cooperative's coordinator, Hajiya Bala, restarts with a stakeholder list. She puts the traders' association chairman in "high power, high interest" because he can effectively block the site. She meets him on Monday. Within an hour they agree to move the stall block back two metres to keep the truck path clear and to give the association three stalls at a reduced rent.

She puts the local government permit officer in "high power, lower interest" and sends him a one-page update every two weeks with photos. She puts the cooperative members in "low power, high interest" and holds a short meeting every Saturday after market. The suppliers go in "monitor", with a message only when orders change.

The change to the plan cost two metres of floor space and three discounted stalls. The cost of finding out later would have been a stopped site and weeks of delay. The same conversation held before the first brick would have cost only the conversation, and the same two metres and three stalls.
:::

## Step 4: Write a communication plan

Knowing who matters is half the work. The other half is deciding how and when you talk to them. A **communication plan** is a simple table answering: who needs what information, how often, by which channel, and from whom.

| Who | What they need | How often | Channel | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sponsor | Progress, risks, decisions needed | Weekly, 10 minutes | Call or voice note + short written update | Project manager |
| Permit officer | Short progress summary with photos | Every two weeks | Email | Project manager |
| Team | What is due this week, who is blocked | Twice a week | WhatsApp group + Saturday meeting | Project manager |
| Traders' association | Changes that affect the road or stalls | When changes happen, plus monthly | Phone call, then message | Coordinator |

Some rules make this table work:

1. **Match the person, not your habit.** A busy executive wants three lines and a decision request. A team wants details. A community wants plain language and a chance to speak.
2. **Use channels people actually use.** If your team lives on WhatsApp, a weekly email may never be read. If a funder requires email for the record, a WhatsApp message is not enough. Use both when you need to.
3. **Send bad news early, in person or by voice if you can, with a proposed fix.** News does not improve by waiting. A sponsor who hears "We are two days behind, and here are two ways to recover" can help. A sponsor who hears about it at the end can only be angry.
4. **Keep a record.** Decisions made in chats vanish. Write the decision in one line and save it in a shared folder.
5. **Do not flood people.** More messages do not mean better communication. Each message should have a purpose: inform, decide or ask.

## When stakeholders disagree

You will meet stakeholders who want conflicting things: the sponsor wants it cheap, the users want extra features, the neighbour wants it quiet. You are not the judge. Make each need visible, link it back to the charter's goal and limits, and escalate the trade-off to whoever has the authority to decide, usually the sponsor. If the charter said the budget is capped, then "more features" has to be paid for with more money or fewer other features. You will practise this in Lesson 14.

:::keyidea
List everyone who can affect or be affected by the project, sort them by power and interest, and give each group the communication it needs, so no one who matters is surprised.
:::

## What you can do now

You can find stakeholders, understand what they want, place them on the grid, choose an approach for each, and write a communication plan. That completes the foundations module. In Lesson 5 you will start planning the work itself, by breaking the scope into pieces small enough to estimate and assign.

:::exercise title=Map your stakeholders
1. Use the project from your Lesson 3 charter, or a new one.
2. List at least eight stakeholders. Include at least one who might be against the project and one who is easy to forget.
3. For each, write what they want in one line.
4. Place each in one of the four boxes. Mark any whose position you are unsure about as "ask".
5. Write a communication table with at least four rows, using the five columns above.
6. Choose the one stakeholder with the most power and talk to them this week. Write down one thing you learned that changed your plan.

A good answer includes at least one surprise: a stakeholder you had not thought of, or a need you had wrong.
:::

modules.title: Planning: scope, time, money and risk

lessons.title: Break the work down: the work breakdown structure
lessons.subtitle: You cannot estimate, schedule or assign a big vague job. You can estimate a small clear one. Learn to cut scope into pieces that work.
outcomes: Build a work breakdown structure from a scope statement
Check a breakdown using the 100 percent rule and the "done" test
Turn the bottom pieces into an activity list with owners
lessons.body:
Tomi says to his team, "Launch the new bakery delivery service by April." Everybody nods. Three weeks later, one person thinks "launch" means a Facebook page, one thinks it means two motorbikes and riders, and one thinks it means a call centre. Nothing is wrong with anyone's effort. The job was too big to see. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

Large jobs hide their parts. The remedy is to cut the work into smaller and smaller pieces until each one is clear, estimable and ownable. That cutting is called building a **work breakdown structure**, or WBS, and it is the single most useful planning tool you will learn.

## What a WBS is

A WBS is a tree. At the top is the whole project. Under it are the main deliverables. Under each deliverable are smaller deliverables, and so on, until the lowest level is small enough to plan well. The lowest pieces are called **work packages**.

Two points are essential.

1. **It lists deliverables, the things that will exist, not just actions.** "Delivery menu printed" is a deliverable. "Print menu" is an action. Deliverables are easier to check, because you can see whether the menu exists. You will turn the deliverables into actions later.
2. **It covers all the work, and only the work in scope.** This is the **100 percent rule**: if you add up everything under a parent, you get the whole parent, with nothing missing and nothing extra. If something is missing, you will meet it later as a surprise. If something extra appears, you are doing out-of-scope work, which wastes money.

:::figure
type: tree
title: A work breakdown for a delivery service launch (invented)
caption: The whole project sits at the top, four main deliverables sit below it, and each splits into smaller deliverables that can be planned and owned. Together the pieces under each parent make up that parent completely.
- Bakery delivery launched | Whole project
  - Delivery team | People ready to deliver
    - Riders hired | Two riders chosen and contracted
    - Riders trained | Handling, safety, customer manners
  - Ordering system | Customers can order and pay
    - Order page live | Simple page or WhatsApp catalogue
    - Payment method set up | Transfer or card link tested
  - Operations | The daily process works
    - Packaging chosen | Boxes that keep goods intact
    - Delivery zones and prices set | Map and rates agreed
  - Marketing | People know about it
    - Launch offer designed | Price, dates, terms
    - Announcement published | Social media and shop
:::

## How to build one

1. **Start from the scope statement and the success criteria** (Lesson 3). Every top-level piece should help meet those.
2. **Write the main deliverables.** Three to eight is a good number for the first level. Ask: "What must exist for the project to be complete?"
3. **Split each deliverable** by asking, "What does this consist of?" Keep going, one level at a time.
4. **Stop at the right size.** When a piece is small enough to estimate with some confidence, give to one person, and clearly mark as done or not done, stop. A common rule of thumb says a work package should take between about 8 hours and 80 hours of effort. That is a guide, not a law. On a small project, a package might be a single day. On a very large one, it might be a few weeks.
5. **Number the pieces** (1, 1.1, 1.1.1) so you can refer to them and track them.
6. **Check completeness** using the 100 percent rule. Read each group and ask, "If all these are done, is the parent done?"

If you prefer, there are two good ways to choose the first-level split: by **deliverable** (what we make), or by **phase** (design, build, test, deliver). Pick whichever makes the project easiest to understand. Do not mix them at the same level, because mixing creates gaps and overlaps.

:::check q5-1
:::

## The "done" test and the owner test

For each work package, answer two questions:

- **Could two different people agree on whether this is finished?** If not, the package is too vague. "Marketing done" fails. "Announcement published on Instagram, Facebook and shop door by 28 March" passes.
- **Can one person be responsible for it?** A package can involve many people, but one name should be on it. If you cannot name an owner, the package is unclear.

## From packages to activities

A WBS says what. A plan also needs how and in what order. For each work package, list the **activities**, the actions required to finish it, along with a rough effort. This activity list feeds directly into scheduling (Lesson 7) and estimating (Lesson 6).

:::example title=From one work package to activities (invented)
**Work package 2.2: Payment method set up.** Done means: a customer can pay for a delivery order using bank transfer or a payment link, and the shop receives and records the money.

Activities:

1. Choose which payment options the shop will accept. (Tomi, 1 hour)
2. Open or confirm the business account and, if using a payment provider, apply for it. Check the provider's current requirements and fees, because these change. (Tomi, 3 hours of work, plus waiting time for approval)
3. Create a simple payment instruction message or link template. (Tomi, 1 hour)
4. Make two test payments of ₦100 and confirm they arrive and can be matched to an order. (Tomi and one friend, 1 hour)
5. Write the steps for recording payments in the sales sheet. (Tomi, 1 hour)

Notice two things. The package has a clear "done". And activity 2 contains waiting time, which does not take Tomi's effort but still takes calendar days. You will deal with that when you build the schedule.
:::

## Common WBS mistakes

- **Making it a to-do list of verbs.** "Call suppliers, buy stuff, tell people" will miss deliverables and hide gaps.
- **Going too deep.** Breaking a two-day job into 40 tiny tasks creates more management work than it saves.
- **Stopping too early.** "Marketing" is not a work package. Nobody can tell what it contains or when it is done.
- **Forgetting management and hidden work.** Meetings, testing, approvals, training, handover and project reporting are real work. Give them their own boxes.
- **Building it alone.** The people who will do the work know what is really involved. Build the WBS with them, even if only on a whiteboard or a group call. A WBS built by one manager in an office tends to miss things the team would catch in five minutes.

:::compare
weak: Social media. Website. Staff. Equipment.
strong: Announcement published on three channels by 28 March (owner: Bisi, 10 hours). Order page live and tested with five trial orders (owner: Tomi, 14 hours).
note: The strong pieces are checkable, have owners and can be estimated.
:::

:::keyidea
Break the scope into deliverables small enough to estimate and own, make sure together they equal the whole project and nothing more, and then list the activities needed to finish each one.
:::

## What you can do now

You can build a WBS from a scope statement, test it with the 100 percent and "done" checks, and turn work packages into activities. In Lesson 6 you will put time and effort numbers on those pieces, including how to estimate when you have never done the work before.

:::exercise title=Build your WBS
1. Use your project from Lessons 3 and 4.
2. Write the top-level deliverables, between three and eight. Check each against your success criteria.
3. Break each deliverable down at least two levels. Stop when a piece passes the "done" test and the owner test.
4. Add at least one box for management work such as meetings, approvals or reporting.
5. Apply the 100 percent rule to every parent: if all children are done, is the parent done? Fix gaps and remove extras.
6. For three work packages, list the activities and a rough estimate of effort in hours.

A good WBS has between 15 and 40 lowest-level pieces for a small project, each with a clear owner. Count yours.
:::

lessons.title: Estimating time and effort honestly
lessons.subtitle: Everyone guesses too low. Learn why, and learn methods that make your guesses much better.
outcomes: Explain why people underestimate and how to correct for it
Use a three-point estimate and the PERT formula
Give an estimate as a range with a stated confidence
lessons.body:
Ask a friend how long it will take to write a ten-page report and they say, "Two days." Ask how long the last report took them and they say, "Oh, about a week, but this one is different." That sentence, "this one is different," is the root of most bad estimates. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

Estimating is not fortune telling. It is a skill with known traps and known fixes. This lesson gives you both.

## Effort, duration and elapsed time are different things

Before you estimate, separate three ideas that people mix up.

- **Effort** is the amount of work, measured in person-hours or person-days. Writing a report might need 12 hours of effort.
- **Duration** is how long the activity takes on the calendar once work starts. If one person works 4 hours a day on it, 12 hours of effort takes 3 working days.
- **Waiting time** is when nothing happens: waiting for approval, delivery, a bank, a reply. It adds calendar days without adding effort.

If you ask for a single number you will not know which kind you got. Ask clearly: "How many hours of work is this, and how many days will it take given your other duties?"

## Why we guess too low

Psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named the **planning fallacy** in 1979: people predict how long their own tasks will take by imagining the smooth path and ignoring how long similar tasks took before. In 1994 Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin and Michael Ross tested it. Students working on their final-year thesis predicted on average about 34 days to finish, and took on average about 55 days. Only about 30 percent finished within the time they had predicted. When asked for their worst-case guess, the average was about 49 days, and still only about half finished by then.

Three habits cause it.

1. **We imagine the plan, not the interruptions.** Nobody pictures the power cut, the sick child, the missing file.
2. **We forget the past.** We treat each project as unique and ignore how similar ones ran.
3. **We are rewarded for optimism.** Saying "two days" pleases the boss today. The bill arrives later.

:::check q6-1
:::

## Five ways to estimate better

**1. Use history first (analogous estimating).** What did the last similar thing actually take? Not what was planned, what it took. If the last event took 6 weeks to organise, start from 6 weeks, then adjust for real differences. If you have no records, start keeping them today. A simple table of "task, estimated, actual" is worth more than any tool.

**2. Look at the outside view.** Bent Flyvbjerg, who studies why big projects overrun, promotes *reference class forecasting*: instead of reasoning only from the details of your project, look at the results of many similar projects and see where yours sits among them. If most comparable website builds run 30 to 50 percent over the first plan, your plan probably needs a margin of that size, whatever it feels like from the inside.

**3. Break it down, then add up (bottom-up estimating).** Use your work breakdown structure. Small pieces are easier to estimate and errors partly cancel out. Do not forget the hidden work: meetings, reviews, fixing, waiting.

**4. Ask the doer.** The person who will do the work gives better numbers than a manager who will not. But check them against history, because doers are often optimistic too.

**5. Give three numbers, not one (three-point estimating).** For each activity ask for:

- **O**, the optimistic time: if almost everything goes right.
- **M**, the most likely time: your honest typical case.
- **P**, the pessimistic time: if several things go wrong, but not a disaster.

Then use the **PERT** weighted average, from the Program Evaluation and Review Technique developed in the 1950s for the US Navy's Polaris missile programme:

**Expected time = (O + 4 x M + P) / 6**

and a rough measure of uncertainty:

**Spread (standard deviation) = (P - O) / 6**

The formula gives most weight to the likely case but pulls the answer toward the pessimistic side whenever the pessimistic number is far from the likely one, which is how real work behaves, because delays are usually longer than savings.

:::example title=Estimating two linked activities (invented numbers)
Tomi needs two things before his bakery delivery launch: an order page, and two riders hired. He asks for three numbers on each.

**Order page live:** O = 2 days, M = 4 days, P = 12 days.
Expected = (2 + 4 x 4 + 12) / 6 = (2 + 16 + 12) / 6 = 30 / 6 = **5 days**.
Spread = (12 - 2) / 6 = 10 / 6, about **1.7 days**.

**Riders hired:** O = 3 days, M = 5 days, P = 13 days.
Expected = (3 + 4 x 5 + 13) / 6 = (3 + 20 + 13) / 6 = 36 / 6 = **6 days**.
Spread = (13 - 3) / 6, about **1.7 days**.

If they must be done one after another, the expected total is 5 + 6 = **11 days**. To combine the uncertainty, do not add the spreads. (The spread is a standard deviation, a measure of how far results typically stray from the average.) Square each, add, then take the square root: 1.7 squared is about 2.9; 2.9 + 2.9 = 5.8; the square root of 5.8 is about **2.4 days**. This assumes the two are independent.

So the honest statement is: "About 11 days, and a roughly one in six chance it takes more than about 13.4 days." Roughly, 84 percent of outcomes fall below the expected time plus one spread. If missing the date hurts badly, quote a date nearer 16 days (expected plus two spreads, about 98 percent). The sponsor can then choose a promise with a known risk instead of a hopeful single number.

Note: the "84 percent" figure treats the outcomes as roughly bell-shaped, which is only an approximation. Use it as a guide to how much margin to add, not as a precise probability.
:::

## Give estimates as ranges

A single number sounds precise and is usually wrong. A range tells the truth. Compare:

:::compare
weak: "It will take 10 days."
strong: "My best guess is 10 days. I am fairly confident it will be between 8 and 15, because the supplier's delivery date is uncertain."
note: The strong version tells the listener where the risk is and invites a decision about it.
:::

Early in a project your ranges should be wide. They should narrow as you learn. If your range stays narrow when you know little, you are bluffing.

## Buffers and where they belong

If every task has its own padding, people use it up (work expands to fill the time) and the project still runs late. A cleaner habit is to estimate each task honestly, with no hidden padding, and then add an explicit, visible **contingency** at project level, sized from your uncertainty, and owned by the manager, not spent task by task. Be open about it: "The expected finish is 14 March. We have added 5 working days of contingency, so we promise 21 March."

## Beware of adding people

If the work is late, adding people feels like the answer. Fred Brooks, who led the development of IBM's OS/360 software and wrote *The Mythical Man-Month* in 1975, observed that adding people to a late software project tends to make it later. New people must be trained, and every extra person adds communication paths. Some tasks cannot be split at all: a baby takes nine months whatever the number of mothers. Where work really can be divided, extra people help. Where it cannot, they do not. Always ask which kind you have.

:::keyidea
Estimate from real past data, ask for optimistic, likely and pessimistic numbers, use (O + 4M + P) / 6, state the answer as a range, and keep contingency visible instead of hiding it in each task.
:::

## What you can do now

You can separate effort from duration, name the planning fallacy, use three-point estimating, and state an estimate as a range with a margin. In Lesson 7 you will use those durations to build a schedule and find the critical path.

:::exercise title=Estimate and then check
1. Pick five tasks from your WBS, or five everyday tasks such as cooking for ten guests, cleaning a house, or preparing a CV.
2. For each write O, M and P, then compute the PERT expected time and spread. Check the arithmetic twice.
3. Do each task over the next few days and record the real time.
4. Compare. Was the real time inside your O to P range? Was it above or below your expected time? Calculate the percentage difference.
5. Write one sentence about your own habit: "I tend to under or over estimate by about ___ percent, mostly because ___."

A good answer uses that percentage as a correction factor on your next set of estimates.
:::

lessons.title: Scheduling: dependencies, the critical path and the Gantt chart
lessons.subtitle: A schedule is not a list of dates. It is a map of what must wait for what. Find the chain that sets your finish date.
outcomes: Link activities with dependencies and spot the ones that wait
Find the critical path and the float of each activity
Read a Gantt chart and explain what it does and does not show
lessons.body:
A caterer in Port Harcourt tells her client, "Your wedding food will be ready by Saturday." She lists the tasks: buy ingredients, cook, pack, deliver, set up. She gives each a day and adds them up. Then the cooking pot supplier cancels. She cannot cook until she gets a pot. She had been tracking days, not links. One broken link, and the whole Saturday promise went with it. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

A schedule begins with one question for every activity: **what has to be finished before this can start?** Answer that for everything and you can see which activities control the finish date, and which ones have room to slip.

## Dependencies

A **dependency** is a link between two activities. The most common kind is **finish to start**: B cannot start until A finishes. You cannot paint a wall until the plaster is dry. There are three other kinds you will meet:

- **Start to start:** B can start once A starts. Two people can begin editing a video chapter once the recording starts.
- **Finish to finish:** B cannot finish until A finishes. Proofreading cannot be completed before the writing is complete.
- **Start to finish:** rare. B cannot finish until A has started. You can ignore this one for now.

Two other terms help. **Lead** lets an activity start a little before its predecessor ends (start painting the first room while the last is still drying). **Lag** adds a forced wait (plaster needs several days to dry before painting). Lag is how you put real waiting time into the plan.

Separate the dependencies by their cause:

- **Hard (logical):** physically impossible any other way. A roof needs walls.
- **Soft (preferred):** you chose the order, but you could change it.
- **External:** depends on someone outside the project: a delivery, a permit, a payment.

External dependencies cause the most surprises. Give them extra attention in your risk list.

## The network and the critical path

Write each activity with its duration and its predecessors. Then draw them as boxes and arrows. This is a **network diagram**. Work forward to find the earliest each activity can start and finish, then work backward from the end to find the latest each can start and finish without delaying the whole project.

:::figure
type: network
title: Which tasks control the finish date (invented project)
caption: Seven activities for opening an online ordering service, with durations in days. The longest chain, Agree scope, Design page, Build page, Test, Launch, takes 14 days and is the critical path. Approvals has 1 day of slack and Train staff has 4.
unit: day
- A | Agree scope | 2 | -
- B | Get approvals | 3 | A
- C | Design page | 4 | A
- D | Build page | 5 | B,C
- E | Test | 2 | D
- F | Train staff | 3 | C
- G | Launch | 1 | E,F
:::

Read the figure like this. A takes 2 days and has nothing before it. After A, two things can start together: getting approvals (3 days) and designing the page (4 days). Building the page (D) needs both. Approvals ends on day 5, but design ends on day 6, so build can only start on day 6. Approvals could slip by one day with no effect. Staff training (F) needs only the design, ends on day 9, and is only needed at launch on day 13, so it has a lot of room.

The chain that decides the end date is the **critical path**: the longest path from start to finish. Here it is A, C, D, E, G: 2 + 4 + 5 + 2 + 1 = **14 days**. Any delay to an activity on that path moves the finish date by the same amount. That is why those activities need your attention first.

**Float**, also called **slack**, is how long an activity can slip without delaying the project. Activities on the critical path have zero float. Approvals (B) has 1 day. Staff training (F) has 4 days.

:::check q7-1
:::

## What to do with this

1. **Protect the critical path.** Put your best people on it. Check these activities daily. Remove their obstacles first.
2. **Use float wisely.** Float is a resource. You can use it to level workloads, for instance by starting training a bit later when people are free. But once float is used, that path can become critical too.
3. **Shorten the project only by shortening the critical path.** Speeding up Approvals does nothing. Two ways to cut the critical path:
   - **Crashing:** add resources, such as extra people or overtime, to the critical activities. This costs more money and, as Lesson 6 showed, does not always work.
   - **Fast tracking:** do activities in parallel that you planned in sequence, such as starting the build while testing the first finished sections. This adds risk of rework.
4. **Recalculate when things change.** The critical path can move. If Design slips from 4 to 7 days, it is still critical. If approvals slip from 3 to 8 days, the critical path jumps to A, B, D, E, G.

:::example title=Reading a change (using the figure above)
The approvals office says it needs 5 days, not 3. Does the launch move?

- Approvals now runs from day 2 to day 7.
- Build needs both approvals and design. Design finishes on day 6, approvals on day 7. Build starts on day 7, not day 6.
- Build runs days 7 to 12, test days 12 to 14, launch ends on day 15.

The project is now 15 days, one day later, because approvals used up its 1 day of float and then went 1 day past it. The critical path has moved to A, B, D, E, G (2 + 5 + 5 + 2 + 1 = 15), and Design Page now has 1 day of float instead of none.

Action: ask whether approvals can be shortened to 4 days, for example by sending the paperwork in the morning and asking the office to review the same day. Or talk to the sponsor about moving the date by a day. The schedule gave you the question before the date was missed.
:::

## The Gantt chart

A **Gantt chart** shows activities as horizontal bars on a calendar. It is named after the American engineer Henry Gantt, who developed charts of this kind in the early 1900s. The Polish engineer Karol Adamiecki had devised a similar chart, which he called a harmonogram, in 1896, but he published mostly in Polish and Russian, so Gantt's name is the one that stuck. A Gantt chart is excellent for showing a schedule to a team or sponsor, because it shows start, finish, overlap, and milestones at a glance.

:::figure
type: gantt
title: The same project as a calendar (invented, in days)
caption: Each bar shows when an activity runs. Critical activities are marked. Approvals and staff training have room to move, while the marked chain finishes the project on day 14.
unit: day
- ! Agree scope | 0 | 2
- Get approvals | 2 | 3 | 1 day of float
- ! Design page | 2 | 4
- ! Build page | 6 | 5
- ! Test | 11 | 2
- Train staff | 6 | 3 | 4 days of float
- ! Launch | 13 | 1
:::

Know its limits. A basic Gantt chart does not always show dependencies clearly, does not show effort, and gives a false sense of precision. A chart with exact bars looks certain, but the numbers inside are estimates. Use it as a view of the plan, not as proof the plan is right.

## Tools

You can do all of this in a spreadsheet. Many free tools also draw Gantt charts and track dependencies. GanttProject is a free desktop application for this. Trello and similar boards are good for task boards but are not true schedulers. Tool features and free limits change, so check the current version before choosing. Whatever you use, the thinking in this lesson is the same.

## Milestones

A **milestone** is a point in time with no duration: "Design approved," "Building handed over". Use milestones for the dates the sponsor cares about and for decisions or approvals. They make a long schedule easier to report on: "We have reached three of five milestones."

:::keyidea
List what each activity must wait for, find the longest chain, which is the critical path, and give that chain your attention first, because any delay on it moves the finish date.
:::

## What you can do now

You can write dependencies, find the critical path and float, read a Gantt chart, and understand what happens when one activity slips. In Lesson 8 you will put money on the plan: estimating cost, building a budget, and tracking it.

:::exercise title=Find your critical path
1. Take 8 to 10 activities from your WBS work packages.
2. For each, write a duration (use your PERT expected time) and the activities it must wait for.
3. Draw the network on paper. Work forward to find the earliest start and finish. Work backward to find the latest.
4. Mark the critical path and write the float for every other activity.
5. Pretend the longest external dependency slips by 3 days. What happens to the finish date?
6. Write the one decision you would make because of what you found.

A good answer names the critical path and gives the finish date with and without the slip.
:::

lessons.title: Budget, cost and resources
lessons.subtitle: Money and people are the other two limits. Learn to price the work, protect against surprises, and have the right people at the right time.
outcomes: Build a bottom-up budget with contingency
Separate direct, indirect, fixed and variable costs
Plan people and other resources so no one is overloaded
lessons.body:
A youth group in Kaduna plans a two-day career fair. The treasurer collects quotes: hall, chairs, sound, snacks. The total fits the sponsor's grant. On the opening morning the generator runs out of fuel, the sound hire company asks for a "late setup fee" nobody had read in the quote, and 60 more students arrive than registered, so snack costs jump. By noon the cash is gone and there is a whole afternoon left. Every item in the budget was real. The budget was missing a plan for the unexpected. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

A good budget does three things: it prices the work honestly, it keeps a visible cushion, and it lets you see during the project whether you are on track.

## Build the budget from the bottom up

Start from your work breakdown structure (Lesson 5). For each work package, list what it needs, estimate the cost, then add up. This is **bottom-up estimating**, and it is more reliable than a single top-down guess ("events like this cost about a million").

For each package, think through four kinds of cost.

1. **People.** Salaries, allowances, freelancers, volunteers' food and transport. Do not treat your own time as free if it is a real limit. Even unpaid work needs a name and an hours estimate.
2. **Materials and equipment.** Things bought or hired.
3. **Services.** Printing, hosting, transport, permits, bank charges.
4. **Other.** Insurance, training, communication costs, fees.

Useful distinctions:

- **Direct costs** belong to this project alone (the hall you hired for it). **Indirect costs** are shared with other work (office rent, a manager's salary shared across projects). Know which your sponsor expects you to include.
- **Fixed costs** do not change with quantity (hall hire is the same for 100 or 200 people). **Variable costs** rise with quantity (meals, printed programmes).

When you gather prices, write down the **date of the quote and how long it is valid**. In an environment where prices move quickly, a quote from three months ago may be useless. Note currency too when something is imported or priced in dollars. If the naira price of an imported item can change before you pay, record that as a risk and add margin or agree a fixed price in writing.

:::example title=A budget with contingency (invented numbers)
The career fair, redone properly. Budget cap from the grant: ₦1,200,000.

| Item | Basis | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Hall, 2 days | Quote dated 3 Feb, valid 30 days | ₦400,000 |
| Catering | 250 guests x ₦1,400 for snack and drink | ₦350,000 |
| Sound and projector | 2-day hire, set-up fee included in the written quote | ₦150,000 |
| Printing and marketing | Banners, flyers, social media boost | ₦100,000 |
| Volunteers and security | Meals, transport, small allowance | ₦80,000 |
| **Subtotal** | | **₦1,080,000** |
| **Contingency, about 11 percent of the subtotal** | For known risks and surprises | **₦120,000** |
| **Total budget** | | **₦1,200,000** |

Check: 400,000 + 350,000 + 150,000 + 100,000 + 80,000 = 1,080,000. Adding 120,000 gives 1,200,000.

The catering line is built on 250 guests, 250 x 1,400 = 350,000. If registration shows 300, the line becomes 420,000, which is 70,000 more. The treasurer writes in the plan: "Above 280 guests, pay the extra catering from contingency, and cap registration at 320." At 320 guests the catering line would be 448,000, which is 98,000 over plan, so this rule would use most of the 120,000 contingency. That is worth knowing before it happens. Now the surprise has a rule before it arrives.
:::

:::check q8-1
:::

## Contingency and management reserve

These two are often confused.

- **Contingency** is money set aside for risks you have identified or can reasonably expect. It is part of the project budget and the project manager controls it. Size it from your risk list (Lesson 9) and the uncertainty in your estimates (Lesson 6). A common range for early-stage projects is somewhere between 10 and 20 percent, but there is no universal number. Higher uncertainty means a bigger cushion.
- **Management reserve** is held by the sponsor for completely unforeseen events. The project manager cannot use it without approval.

Tell your sponsor which you are using. Hiding contingency inside every line makes the budget impossible to read. Showing it on its own line keeps the discussion honest.

## Cash flow, not just total cost

A budget says how much. A **cash flow** plan says when money leaves and arrives. A project can be within budget and still fail because a payment is due before the grant arrives. For each large cost, write the date it must be paid, and compare with the dates money comes in. Where there is a gap, you need a deposit schedule, a smaller first payment, or a bridge.

## How you are paid changes your risk

If you work as a freelancer or contractor, the type of contract matters.

- **Fixed price:** you agree one price for a defined scope. If your estimate is too low, you lose. Clear scope (Lesson 3) is your protection.
- **Time and materials:** you are paid for the hours and costs you actually use, often at agreed rates. Risk sits with the client. Many clients want a cap.
- **Cost plus:** the client pays your actual costs plus a fee or a percentage. Common in large public projects, less common for small ones.

Whichever you use, put changes of scope in writing with the price effect. "We can add the second language version for an extra ₦80,000 and three more days" is a normal sentence, not an awkward one.

## Plan the people

Money is one limit. People's time is another, and often the real one.

1. **List the skills the project needs.** Not names yet: skills.
2. **Match people to work packages.** Find who has the skill and the time.
3. **Check availability honestly.** Someone who works 40 hours a week on other duties cannot give you 40 hours. If a person has two other jobs, five hours a week may be their actual limit.
4. **Look for overload.** Sum each person's hours by week. If someone is assigned 55 hours in a week, the plan is broken, whatever the Gantt chart says. Fix it by moving non-critical work into its float (Lesson 7), adding help, or moving the date.
5. **Plan for gaps.** Holidays, exams, religious observances, travel and sickness are all predictable somewhere in a long project. Check the calendar.

Physical resources work the same way: one projector cannot be in two halls. A single shared machine can be your hidden critical path.

:::figure
type: bars
title: Where the career fair money goes (invented)
caption: A budget of about 1.2 million naira, with the biggest slices going to the hall and the catering. The contingency of 120,000 is highlighted as its own line, separate from the planned costs.
unit: naira
- Hall | 400000
- Catering | 350000
- Sound and projector | 150000
- Printing and marketing | 100000
- Volunteers and security | 80000
- ! Contingency | 120000
:::

:::keyidea
Build the budget bottom-up from the work breakdown, show contingency openly as its own line, plan when money moves, and check that the people you need actually have the hours.
:::

## What you can do now

You can build a budget from work packages, choose and size contingency, understand contract types, plan cash flow, and check people for overload. In Lesson 9 you will deal with the thing contingency is for: risk.

:::exercise title=Price your project
1. Take your WBS and choose ten work packages.
2. For each, write the people, materials, services and other costs. Note the date of each price you collect and when it expires.
3. Add up a subtotal. Decide a contingency percentage and justify it in one sentence based on how uncertain your estimates are.
4. Mark which costs are fixed and which vary with quantity. Write one rule like the catering rule above for the most variable cost.
5. List each person involved and their real weekly hours. Find the busiest week and check for overload.
6. Write a one-line cash flow note: the largest payment, when it is due, and where the money comes from.

A good result has a total, a visible contingency line, and at least one rule for what happens if a variable cost grows.
:::

lessons.title: Managing risk before it manages you
lessons.subtitle: You cannot remove uncertainty, but you can see it coming. Learn to find, rank and answer risks while they are still cheap to handle.
outcomes: Identify risks using a pre-mortem and a checklist
Rank risks by likelihood and impact and calculate expected cost
Choose a response and write a usable risk register
lessons.body:
A small construction firm in Lagos is two weeks from handing over a block of flats. The electrician asks for the cable delivery to be confirmed. The site manager says, "It is coming." It does not come. The supplier had switched the order to another customer the month before. The cable is a three-week wait. If anyone had asked at the start, "What could stop this handover?", the single-supplier cable order would have been on the list, and a second supplier could have been named in an afternoon. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

A **risk** is an uncertain event that, if it happens, affects your project's goals. It has not happened yet. An **issue** is a risk that has already happened, or a problem that is certain. Risk management is the habit of dealing with the first kind so that you have fewer of the second.

Risks can be good as well as bad. A **threat** hurts the project, such as a supplier delay. An **opportunity** helps, such as a client offering a bigger venue for free. A mature plan watches for both.

## Step 1: Find the risks

Do not rely on one person's worry. Use several methods.

1. **The pre-mortem.** Gather the team and say: "Imagine it is the end date, and the project failed badly. Write down why." Psychologist Gary Klein popularised this technique. Because people imagine a failure as already real, they speak more freely than when asked, "What might go wrong?" Ten minutes with sticky notes or a shared document usually produces a long list.
2. **Walk through the WBS.** For each work package ask, "What could make this late, expensive or poor?"
3. **Review your assumptions** (Lesson 3). Each assumption is a possible risk.
4. **Check external dependencies** (Lesson 7). Suppliers, approvals and payments top most lists.
5. **Use a prompt list.** Think through people (illness, loss of a key person), money (late payment, price rises), technology (failure, power cuts, poor internet), suppliers, regulation, weather, and the sponsor (changed priorities).
6. **Learn from the past.** What went wrong in similar projects? Ask someone who did one.

:::check q9-1
:::

## Step 2: Rank them

You cannot respond to everything. Rank each risk on two scales.

- **Likelihood**: how probable? Use simple levels (low, medium, high) or percentages (10, 30, 60).
- **Impact**: how much would it hurt? Think of cost, days of delay and quality.

Placing risks on a grid shows where to put your effort.

:::figure
type: matrix
title: Likelihood and impact
caption: Risks that are both likely and severe need action first. Unlikely but severe risks need a backup plan, likely but small risks need a routine fix, and unlikely small risks can be watched.
x: Likelihood | Unlikely | Likely
y: Impact | Small impact | Big impact
tl: Plan a backup | Rare but costly, so prepare a fallback
tr: Act first | Likely and costly, so reduce it now
bl: Watch | Note it and look again later
br: Handle by routine | Common and minor, so build a habit
hot: tr
:::

Where you can, turn the numbers into money. The **expected cost** of a risk is its probability multiplied by its cost if it happens.

**Expected cost = probability x impact (in money)**

A risk with a 30 percent chance of costing ₦200,000 has an expected cost of 0.30 x 200,000 = ₦60,000. That figure does not predict what will happen; it is a way to compare risks and to size your contingency (Lesson 8). A 5 percent chance of a ₦2,000,000 loss has an expected cost of ₦100,000, larger than the first, though it feels less urgent. But expected cost does not tell the whole story: some losses are too big to survive however unlikely they are, and for those you plan a defence regardless of the number.

## Step 3: Choose a response

For each important threat, choose one of four main responses.

- **Avoid.** Change the plan so the risk cannot happen. Drop the risky supplier. Choose a different venue.
- **Mitigate.** Reduce the likelihood or impact. Order cable early. Test the generator before the event. Train a second person on the critical skill.
- **Transfer.** Move the financial effect to someone else, for example through insurance or a fixed-price contract. The risk still exists, but someone else pays for it. Check the terms carefully, because transfer is only as good as the contract.
- **Accept.** Do nothing now, because the cost of acting is greater than the risk. Acceptance can be passive (do nothing) or active (set aside contingency money or time for it).

For opportunities the matching responses are to **exploit** (make it certain), **enhance** (raise its chance or benefit), **share** (partner with someone better placed), or **accept**.

Also decide a **trigger**: the early warning sign that the risk is becoming real. "The cable supplier has not replied to two messages by Friday" is a trigger. Pair each trigger with a planned action so you do not have to decide under pressure.

## Step 4: Write it down and keep it alive

Put risks in a **risk register**, a simple table.

| ID | Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Expected cost | Response | Trigger | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Every risk needs an **owner**, one named person responsible for watching and acting. A risk everyone owns is a risk no one owns. Review the register briefly at every status meeting. Retire risks that have passed, add new ones, and move any that have occurred into the issue list.

:::example title=A mini risk register (invented, for the career fair)
| ID | Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Expected cost | Response | Trigger | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Generator fails or runs out of fuel | 30% | ₦80,000 | ₦24,000 | Mitigate: service it, buy fuel for both days, ask the hall if mains has a backup | No test run done by day -3 | Bola |
| R2 | Registered guests exceed 280 | 40% | ₦70,000 (at 300 guests) | ₦28,000 | Accept with a rule: above 280 guests pay the extra catering from contingency, and cap registration at 320 | Registration passes 260 | Treasurer |
| R3 | Main speaker cancels | 10% | ₦150,000 | ₦15,000 | Mitigate: name a reserve speaker in advance | No written confirmation by day -7 | Chair |
| R4 | Sound company adds hidden fees | 20% | ₦40,000 | ₦8,000 | Avoid: get all fees in writing before signing | Quote lacks line for setup fee | Treasurer |

The expected costs add up to 24,000 + 28,000 + 15,000 + 8,000 = **₦75,000**, which sits inside the ₦120,000 contingency of Lesson 8. But an expected cost is an average, not a guarantee. Also look at the worst single risk (here the ₦150,000 speaker loss) and ask whether the cushion could survive it. Had the total been ₦200,000, the treasurer would know the cushion was too thin before spending a naira.
:::

## Habits that make risk work

- **Do it early and repeat.** A risk list written once and filed is a decoration. Review it weekly.
- **Be specific.** "Supplier problems" is not a risk. "Cable supplier may reallocate our order because we have no written confirmation" is.
- **Separate cause, event and effect.** "Because we have a single supplier (cause), the cable may not arrive (event), which would delay handover by three weeks (effect)." Fixing the cause is usually the best response.
- **Do not hide bad news.** The most dangerous risks are the ones people are afraid to mention. Make it safe to say them.

:::compare
