weak: "Risk: things might go wrong with suppliers. Owner: team."
strong: "R7: Our only cable supplier may reassign our order, causing a three-week delay. Likelihood 30%, impact ₦400,000. Response: name a second supplier and place a deposit order by 15 March. Trigger: no written delivery date by 1 March. Owner: Emeka."
note: The strong version can be acted on by someone who was not in the meeting.
:::

:::keyidea
Find risks early with a pre-mortem and checklists, rank them by likelihood and impact, choose a response with an owner and a trigger, and review the register every week.
:::

## What you can do now

You can find, rank and respond to risks, calculate expected cost and write a risk register. That completes the planning module: scope, work, time, money, people and risk. Module 3 starts with the part many beginners find hardest: leading the people who will do the work.

:::exercise title=Run a pre-mortem
1. Take your project and imagine it is the finish date and it has failed. Spend ten minutes writing every reason, with no editing. Aim for at least fifteen.
2. Merge duplicates and turn each into a specific risk using "cause, event, effect".
3. Estimate likelihood and impact for each. Calculate expected cost for the top five.
4. For each of the top five, choose one of the four responses, write a trigger and name an owner.
5. Add the expected costs of the top five and compare with your contingency from Lesson 8. Is the cushion big enough?

A good answer gives one change you would make to the plan right now because of the register.
:::

lessons.title: Lead the team: roles, trust and how groups develop
lessons.subtitle: A plan does not do work. People do. Learn how teams form, how to give clear responsibilities, and how to lead people you cannot order around.
outcomes: Describe the stages teams pass through and what to do in each
Assign clear roles using a RACI chart
Delegate and motivate without relying on authority
lessons.body:
Chinedu is a good accountant. His company makes him project manager for a new customer portal, with a team of six from IT, sales and customer service. None of them reports to him. In week one he sends a task list by email. By week three half the tasks are untouched, two people are quietly angry about a decision nobody discussed, and one has stopped replying. Chinedu's list was fine. What he lacked was the second job of a project manager: leading people, often without being their boss. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

## Teams go through stages

In 1965 psychologist Bruce Tuckman published a review of research on small groups in the journal *Psychological Bulletin*. He described four stages groups tend to pass through. In 1977, with Mary Ann Jensen, he added a fifth after reviewing later studies. The model is widely taught because it matches what many people have lived.

:::figure
type: cycle
title: How teams develop
caption: Tuckman's stages are forming, storming, norming and performing, followed by adjourning when the work ends. Teams do not always move in a straight line, and a new member or a big change can send a team back a stage.
center: Team
- Forming | Polite, unsure, looking to the leader
- Storming | Disagreement about roles and methods
- Norming | Agreeing how to work together
- Performing | Working well, solving problems together
- Adjourning | Finishing, recognising, letting go
:::

What it looks like and what to do:

- **Forming.** People are polite and uncertain. They want to know the goal, their role and the rules. Your job: be clear, welcome everyone, explain the purpose and give early direction.
- **Storming.** Disagreements surface about who decides, how to work, who does what. It is uncomfortable and normal. Do not panic and do not suppress it. Your job: bring conflict into the open, return to the goals in the charter, and set clear decision rules.
- **Norming.** The team agrees on how it works: meeting habits, communication, standards. Your job: reinforce the habits that work, and start stepping back.
- **Performing.** The team solves problems with little direction. Your job: remove obstacles, protect them from interference, and watch for complacency.
- **Adjourning.** The project ends. People can feel loss or fear for their next job. Your job: celebrate, give honest recognition, and help people move on (Lesson 15).

Notice the main point. Storming is not evidence that you chose the wrong team. It is part of the road, and a team that seems to skip it may be hiding its disagreements.

:::check q10-1
:::

## What makes teams work

Google ran a research effort called Project Aristotle to find out why some of its teams did better than others, and published its findings on its re:Work site, with the page originally published in 2015. It reported that who was on the team mattered less than how the team worked together. The five factors it identified are listed in order of importance, and the first was **psychological safety**: team members feel safe to take risks, ask questions, admit mistakes and disagree without being embarrassed or punished. The other four were dependability (people do what they say), structure and clarity (clear goals, roles and plans), meaning (the work matters to the people doing it), and impact (they believe it makes a difference).

You do not need Google's resources to use this. Ways to build it in an ordinary team:

- **Admit your own mistakes first.** If the leader says "I got that estimate wrong," others learn that mistakes are survivable.
- **Respond well to bad news.** If the person who reports a problem gets blamed, you will not hear about the next one.
- **Ask for opinions, then use them.** Asking and ignoring is worse than not asking.
- **Make goals and roles visible.** People cannot be dependable when they do not know what they are responsible for.

## Roles and the RACI chart

Many conflicts come from unclear ownership. A **RACI chart** is a simple grid of tasks against people, showing who does what in four letters:

- **R: Responsible.** Does the work.
- **A: Accountable.** Owns the result and has the final say. Only one person per task.
- **C: Consulted.** Gives input before decisions. Two-way conversation.
- **I: Informed.** Told after the decision. One-way.

:::example title=A RACI chart for the portal project (invented)

| Task | Chinedu (PM) | Amina (IT) | Kola (Sales) | Ife (Support) | Dr Okafor (Sponsor) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Agree list of portal features | R | C | C | C | A |
| Build login and account pages | I | A, R | C | I | I |
| Write help guides | C | I | I | A, R | I |
| Test with 10 customers | A | R | C | R | I |
| Approve launch date | R | C | C | C | A |

How to read it: Amina is accountable and responsible for building. Ife owns the help guides. Dr Okafor approves the feature list and launch date, and Chinedu does the legwork of preparing those decisions. Each row has exactly one A and at least one R.

Check for problems: a row with no R means nobody does it. A row with two A's means two people will each assume the other decided. A person with R on every row is overloaded. A row where everybody is C means a slow decision.
:::

Build the chart with the team in a meeting. People accept roles they helped define.

## Delegate properly

Delegating means handing over responsibility, not just a task. Four rules:

1. **Say the outcome, not the method.** "The login page must let a user reset a password in under two minutes" works better than a list of steps, unless the method truly matters.
2. **Give authority with responsibility.** If you give a task but not the access, budget or decision rights to do it, it will stall.
3. **Agree the check-in points.** Not constant monitoring. "Show me a draft on Wednesday" prevents surprises without breathing down their neck.
4. **Match the level of control to the person.** A newcomer to the skill needs more direction and more frequent check-ins. An expert needs clarity on the outcome and room to work.

## Leading without authority

Most project managers do not control their team's pay, promotion or daily instructions. You lead through:

- **Clarity.** People follow a clear picture of the goal and their part in it.
- **Credibility.** Do what you say, tell the truth, know your plan.
- **Relationships.** Talk to people one-to-one early, learn what they care about, and ask what they need to succeed.
- **Fairness.** Share credit publicly, give criticism privately, treat people the same way.
- **Linking to their boss.** If team members' managers set their priorities, talk to those managers early. Their buy-in affects their staff's time.

Different motives drive different people. Some care about learning, some about recognition, some about stability, some about helping others. Ask rather than guess. Money and conditions do matter, so do not pretend otherwise, but you can often influence meaning, clarity and recognition even where you cannot change pay.

:::compare
weak: "Everyone, here are your tasks. Deliver by Friday."
strong: "Here is why this matters to the client and what a good result looks like. Which part do you want to own, and what do you need from me to finish it by Friday?"
note: The strong version builds ownership and surfaces obstacles early.
:::

:::keyidea
Lead by making goals and roles clear, building a team where people can speak up, expecting a rough storming stage, and giving each task exactly one accountable owner.
:::

## What you can do now

You can describe team stages and respond to each, build a RACI chart, delegate an outcome, and lead people you do not manage. In Lesson 11 you will learn the day-to-day mechanics of delivering work, using the two most popular agile approaches, Scrum and Kanban.

:::exercise title=Build a RACI and have one hard conversation
1. List at least six tasks or decisions from your project and at least four people or roles.
2. Fill in a RACI chart. Check: exactly one A in each row, at least one R, nobody with R on everything.
3. Pick one person who has an unclear role or a possible disagreement. Write three questions you would ask them in a one-to-one conversation, such as "What would make this project a success for you?" and "What worries you about your part?"
4. Hold the conversation, or practise it aloud with a friend. Write down one thing you heard that you did not expect.
5. Decide which Tuckman stage your group is probably in and write one action that suits that stage.

A good answer shows a RACI with no gaps and one concrete change you made after listening.
:::

lessons.title: Running the work: Scrum and Kanban in practice
lessons.subtitle: Two light methods used far beyond software. Learn how a Sprint runs, how a Kanban board limits chaos, and how to borrow from both.
outcomes: Describe the roles, events and artifacts of Scrum
Set up a Kanban board with limits on work in progress
Choose which to use, or combine them, for a given team
lessons.body:
A four-person design studio in Abuja has the same problem every week. Everyone is "working on" six things. Clients ask for updates, and nobody can say what is truly finished. Friday arrives with a lot of half-done work and an exhausted team. They do not need a bigger plan. They need a rhythm and a way to see the work. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

Scrum and Kanban are two of the most widely used ways to get that. Both come from software and manufacturing, but both now run marketing teams, schools, event planners and design studios. Both are short, and both are easy to misuse. This lesson explains how they really work.

## Scrum in plain words

Scrum is a framework described in the *Scrum Guide*, written by Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland. The current version is the 2020 edition, and it is free to read online. Its core idea is to work in fixed, short cycles, deliver something usable each time, and use what you learn to improve.

**Sprints.** The work happens in **Sprints**, which the Guide says are fixed-length events of one month or less. Many teams choose one or two weeks. A Sprint has a goal. When one Sprint ends, the next begins straight away.

**Three accountabilities.** The Scrum Guide defines three, all together called the Scrum Team:

- **The Product Owner** decides what is most valuable to build and maintains the ordered list of work. One person, who talks to the users and sponsors.
- **The Developers** do the work to create the result. In the Guide's sense, "developers" means whoever builds each increment, including designers and writers, not only programmers.
- **The Scrum Master** helps the team follow Scrum, removes obstacles and coaches. It is not a boss or a project manager in the traditional sense.

**Three artifacts, each with a commitment:**

- **Product Backlog**, an ordered list of everything that might be needed, with the **Product Goal** as its commitment.
- **Sprint Backlog**, the items chosen for this Sprint plus a plan, with the **Sprint Goal** as its commitment.
- **Increment**, a usable piece of the result, with the **Definition of Done** as its commitment. The Definition of Done is the shared checklist for what "finished" means.

**Five events:** the Sprint itself, plus four inside it.

:::figure
type: cycle
title: One Sprint
caption: Each Sprint begins with planning, continues with daily check-ins, and ends with a review of the finished work and a retrospective on how the team worked, then the next Sprint starts.
center: Sprint
- Sprint Planning | Choose the goal and the work
- Daily Scrum | A 15-minute check-in on progress
- Build the Increment | Do the work to the Definition of Done
- Sprint Review | Show the result, get feedback
- Retrospective | Improve how we work
:::

- **Sprint Planning:** the team decides what it can deliver and how. The Guide sets a maximum of eight hours for a one-month Sprint, shorter for shorter Sprints.
- **Daily Scrum:** a 15-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adjust the plan for the next day. It is for the team, not a status report to a manager.
- **Sprint Review:** the team shows what it finished to stakeholders and collects feedback, which updates the Product Backlog.
- **Sprint Retrospective:** the team looks at how it worked, such as people, process and tools, and picks improvements. The Guide gives a maximum of three hours for a one-month Sprint.

:::check q11-1
:::

:::example title=One Sprint for the bakery order page (invented)
Tomi's bakery team uses one-week Sprints. Tomi is Product Owner. Bisi and Seun build the page. Ada, a friend who has done this before, acts as Scrum Master for two hours a week.

**Product Goal:** customers order and pay for bakery items by WhatsApp or a simple page, with 20 orders a week within two months.

**Monday, Sprint Planning (45 minutes).** Product Backlog top items: show the menu with prices, add an order form, accept payment by transfer, send a confirmation message. The team sets a **Sprint Goal**: "A customer can see the menu and place an order." They pick the first two items.

**Tuesday to Thursday.** Fifteen-minute Daily Scrum at 9:00. On Wednesday Seun says the photo upload keeps failing. Ada helps him find a lighter image size.

**Definition of Done** (agreed earlier): works on a phone, tested with two real orders, prices checked against the price list, no broken links.

**Friday, Review (30 minutes).** They show a real order being placed. Two friends test it. One says the "Add" button is too small for thumbs. Tomi adds that to the backlog.

**Friday, Retrospective (20 minutes).** Keep: the 9:00 check-in. Change: write the task size down before starting, since photo upload took twice the guess. Next Sprint starts Monday.

The team delivered something real in a week, learned from real users, and corrected a habit.
:::

## Kanban in plain words

Kanban comes from the Japanese for "signboard". It grew out of Toyota's manufacturing system and was adapted for knowledge work. *The Kanban Guide*, written by Daniel Vacanti and Yuval Yeret (2020, free at kanbanguides.org), describes three core practices: defining and visualising a workflow, actively managing the items in it, and improving it. Limiting work in progress is a central part of managing the flow.

A **Kanban board** has columns for each stage of your process, such as To do, Doing, Review, Done. Each work item is a card. Cards move from left to right.

The key practice is the **WIP limit**, a cap on how many items can be in a stage at once. WIP means work in progress. If "Doing" is limited to three, then when it has three cards, nobody starts a fourth. They finish or help finish one first.

Why does that help? Look at what happens without a limit. People start new work whenever they feel blocked or bored, so many items stay half-done at the same time. Each item then takes much longer to finish, and little reaches the customer. A limit forces finishing before starting and exposes bottlenecks, since a full column shows where work is piling up.

There is a simple relationship called **Little's Law**: on average, the time an item takes from start to finish equals the number of items in progress divided by how many you finish per period.

**Average time to finish = work in progress / throughput**

If the studio always has 12 jobs in progress and finishes 3 per week, an average job takes 12 / 3 = 4 weeks. If they cut WIP to 6 and still finish 3 per week, the average drops to 6 / 3 = 2 weeks. The same people, the same output, and every client gets their job in half the time. This works when throughput stays steady, which is why WIP limits are worth testing, not just believing.

Useful measures on a Kanban board are **cycle time** (how long an item takes from start to finish), **throughput** (how many items you finish per week) and **work item age** (how long an unfinished item has been in progress). They come from the board itself, with no special tools.

## Scrum or Kanban, or both?

| | Scrum | Kanban |
|---|---|---|
| Rhythm | Fixed Sprints | Continuous flow |
| Planning | At the start of each Sprint | Whenever there is capacity |
| Roles | Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers | None required |
| Main control | Sprint Goal and time box | WIP limits |
| Good for | Building a product in steps with regular feedback | Steady streams of requests, support, maintenance, mixed work |

Scrum suits a team building something new where the work can be planned in short rounds. Kanban suits teams whose work arrives unpredictably, such as a support desk or an agency handling client requests. Many teams combine them, running Sprints and also using a board with WIP limits. A board is almost always a good idea, whatever method you use.

## Warning signs

- **Ceremonies with no point.** If the Daily Scrum becomes a status report to the boss, you are keeping the form without the purpose.
- **Never finishing.** If Sprint after Sprint ends with half-done work, your Definition of Done is unclear, your plans are too big, or too many things are happening at once.
- **A board that is a decoration.** If cards do not move in real time, it tells nobody anything.
- **Using it as an excuse.** "We are agile" does not remove the need for a goal, a budget, or a date the sponsor can trust (Lesson 2).

:::keyidea
Scrum gives you a rhythm of short cycles ending in usable work and honest review, and Kanban gives you a board with limits on work in progress, and both succeed by finishing things before starting new ones.
:::

## What you can do now

You can name Scrum's roles, artifacts and events, set up a Kanban board with WIP limits, use Little's Law to explain why limits help, and choose between the two. In Lesson 12 you will learn the communication habits that keep a project informed, starting with meetings that do not waste time.

:::exercise title=Set up a one-week experiment
1. List 10 things you or your team need to do in the next two weeks.
2. Draw a board with at least three columns: To do, Doing, Done. Put a WIP limit of two or three on Doing. You can use paper, a wall of sticky notes, or a free tool such as Trello. Check the tool's current free plan before you rely on it.
3. Write a Definition of Done for the two most important items.
4. Work for one week, respecting the limit. At the end, count how many items reached Done and how long each took.
5. Write down one change you would make to the limit or the board for the second week.

A good answer reports what happened, even if the experiment felt awkward, and states one specific change.
:::

lessons.title: Meetings, updates and clear communication
lessons.subtitle: Most project managers spend more time communicating than doing anything else. Make every meeting and message earn its place.
outcomes: Run a short meeting that ends with decisions and owners
Write a status update a busy sponsor can use in two minutes
Communicate well in remote and WhatsApp-heavy teams
lessons.body:
A manufacturing firm in Ikeja holds a Monday project meeting. It is scheduled for an hour and always runs ninety minutes. Eleven people attend. The first twenty minutes are spent waiting for latecomers. Three people speak for most of the rest. At the end, nobody can say what was decided, and on Thursday two people discover they both thought the other would order the part. The meeting felt like work. It produced almost none. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

Communication is the nervous system of a project. Done badly, it burns hours and still leaves people in the dark. Done well, it is short, regular and useful. This lesson gives you the tools.

## Why a meeting exists

Before you invite anyone, ask what the meeting is for. There are only a few good reasons:

- **To decide something** that needs several people's input.
- **To solve a problem** that benefits from different views at once.
- **To align** on a plan or a change where tone and questions matter.
- **To build the team** when people have not met.

If the aim is only to share information that could be read in two minutes, send a message instead. Reading is quicker than listening, and people can do it when they want.

## A meeting that works

1. **State the purpose and the decision needed in the invite.** "Decide which supplier for the cable order" is a purpose. "Project catch-up" is not.
2. **Invite only the people needed.** Anyone who is only "informed" can read the notes. Fewer people means faster decisions.
3. **Prepare an agenda with times.** Send any reading in advance.
4. **Start on time.** Every time you wait for latecomers, you teach people that being late is acceptable.
5. **Decide how to decide.** Who has the final say? If there is a disagreement, will you vote, or will the accountable person choose after hearing everyone? Say so before the argument starts.
6. **Capture decisions, actions and owners live.** Someone writes them in view of everyone. Each action has a name and a date.
7. **End by reading the actions back.** Thirty seconds. This one habit catches most misunderstandings.
8. **Send the notes the same day.** Three lines are enough: decisions, actions with owners and dates, questions still open.

:::check q12-1
:::

For a regular team check-in, such as the Daily Scrum from Lesson 11, keep it short enough to stand through. Fifteen minutes is a good guide. Three useful questions are: What moved forward? What is blocking you? What do you need from someone here?

## The status update

Your sponsor and other senior stakeholders (Lesson 4) need to know three things: where are we, are we going to be okay, and do you need anything from me. A good **status update** answers those on one page or in one short message.

Use a consistent layout so people learn where to look. A traffic-light status is common: **green** (on track), **amber** (at risk, with a plan), **red** (off track, help needed). Always say why, and never use green to mean "I do not want to worry you".

:::example title=A two-minute status update (invented project)
**Career fair: status as of Friday 21 February**

**Overall: AMBER.** Date and budget still holding. One risk needs a decision.

**Done this week:** Hall booking confirmed in writing. Speaker line-up finished (6 of 6). Sound quote received with the setup fee shown.

**Next week:** Open registration on Monday. Print banners. Test the generator.

**Schedule:** On track for 14 March. Critical path is registration to catering numbers.

**Budget:** ₦612,000 committed of ₦1,200,000. Contingency ₦120,000 untouched.

**Risks and issues:**
- Registration may exceed 280. Plan: above 280 guests, pay the extra catering from contingency, and cap registration at 320. *Decision needed from the chair by Wednesday: confirm the cap.*
- Generator not yet tested. Owner Bola, test on 7 March.

**Help needed:** The chair's confirmation of the registration cap.

This takes two minutes to read, ends with a clear ask, and tells the reader exactly what to do.
:::

Good updates share three habits. They are **honest**: amber means amber. They are **consistent**: same day, same format, so nobody has to chase you. And they **end with a request** when you need a decision, because information without a decision rarely changes anything.

## Writing messages people act on

Many project messages fail because the reader cannot tell what they are being asked. Put the point first.

:::compare
weak: "Hi, just following up on the thing from last week. Let me know your thoughts when you can. Thanks!"
strong: "Hi Amaka, I need you to confirm by Wednesday 5 pm whether the banner design is approved, so printing can start on Thursday. The design is attached. If I do not hear from you by then, I will treat design A as approved, as we agreed on Monday."
note: The strong message names the person, the question, the deadline, and what will happen next. It also says what will happen if there is no reply. Use a default like this only if it was agreed in advance, and choose one that costs little if it turns out wrong.
:::

A few more habits:

- **One message, one purpose.** If you need three decisions, number them.
- **Say the date, not "soon".** "By Wednesday 5 pm" can be followed. "Soon" cannot.
- **Write in plain words.** Jargon makes people nod and misunderstand. If you use a term, explain it once.
- **Do not hide critical news in a group chat.** Important things go to a named person directly and are then recorded.

## Remote teams and WhatsApp

Many Nigerian teams run on WhatsApp, with some people in different cities and time zones. It is fast and everyone has it, but it also loses decisions in a stream of messages. Practical rules:

- **Separate groups by purpose.** One group for urgent work, one for social chat if needed, so serious messages are not buried.
- **Pin or copy decisions** to a shared document with a date. A team decision lost on page 40 of a chat is a decision that did not happen.
- **Agree response times.** "Urgent: call. Normal: reply within a working day." Expectations stop people feeling ignored.
- **Respect time and data.** Voice notes help for nuance, but not everyone can play them at work. Offer a short written summary. Be careful with data costs and with connectivity: share files in small sizes where needed.
- **Use video for the hard conversations.** Disagreements and sensitive news go badly in text.

Whichever tools you use, a **decision log** is a quick habit worth having: a simple table with the date, the decision, who made it and why. When someone asks six weeks later, "Why did we choose this supplier?", the answer takes ten seconds.

:::keyidea
Hold meetings only to decide, solve or align, end them with actions and owners read aloud, and send short, regular, honest updates that finish with the decision you need.
:::

## What you can do now

You can design and run an effective meeting, write a status update that gets used, send messages that people act on, and handle remote work. In Lesson 13 you will learn how to track progress against your plan with real numbers, and how to handle changes without losing control.

:::exercise title=Run one short meeting and send one update
1. Choose a real group, such as your team, family committee or study group, with a decision to make.
2. Write an invite with a purpose line that names the decision. Add three agenda items with times.
3. Run the meeting for 30 minutes or less. Write decisions and actions in view of the group. Read the actions back at the end.
4. Send notes within a few hours.
5. Write a one-page status update for a sponsor or an imagined sponsor, using the layout in this lesson. End with a specific ask.
6. After a week, check how many of the actions were done and note what helped or hindered.

A good answer shows a purpose line with a decision in it and a status update that ends with a clear request.
:::

lessons.title: Track progress and control change
lessons.subtitle: A plan only helps if you compare it with reality. Learn to measure progress honestly, use earned value, and handle change requests without losing control.
outcomes: Measure progress in ways that are hard to fake
Calculate and interpret earned value measures
Run a simple change control process and avoid scope creep
lessons.body:
"How is the project going?" asks the sponsor. "Good, about 80 percent done," says the manager. Two weeks later: "About 80 percent done." Two weeks after that: "Still about 80 percent." This is called the **90 percent syndrome**, and it is a common way projects lie to themselves. The last stretch of work always seems to be nearly finished, because "percent done" was a feeling, not a measurement. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

Monitoring and controlling means three steps repeated all through the project: **measure** what is really happening, **compare** with the plan, and **act** on the difference. This lesson gives you tools for all three.

## Set a baseline

You cannot measure a gap without something to measure against. Once your plan is agreed (scope, schedule, budget), save it as the **baseline**. After that, you do not quietly edit the plan when things slip. You keep the baseline, record what really happens, and change the baseline only through a formal decision. The difference between baseline and reality is called **variance**.

## Measure progress honestly

Avoid "I feel it is 80 percent done". Use measures that are hard to bend.

1. **Done or not done.** For each work package with a clear definition of done (Lesson 5), the count of finished packages is a solid measure. A package that is "almost done" counts as not done.
2. **Weighted milestones.** Give a package credit only at fixed points: 0 percent at start, 50 percent when the first draft is reviewed, 100 percent when accepted. This stops optimistic guessing.
3. **Remaining effort.** Ask the person doing the work, "How many more hours until it is done?" instead of "What percent is done?". People are more honest about what is left.
4. **Burn-up or burn-down charts** in agile teams: plot work finished (or remaining) against time and see whether the line is heading to the target.

Compare **planned versus actual** often, at least weekly for short projects. Look at three things: schedule (are we where we should be?), cost (have we spent what we planned for this much progress?) and quality (does what we have done pass the checks?).

## Earned value: one way to read cost and schedule together

Looking at schedule and cost separately can mislead. If you have spent 60 percent of your budget, is that good or bad? It depends on how much work is finished. **Earned value management** (EVM) uses three numbers to answer.

- **Planned value (PV):** the budgeted cost of the work that should be done by today according to the plan.
- **Earned value (EV):** the budgeted cost of the work actually done by today.
- **Actual cost (AC):** what you have actually spent so far.

From these:

- **Schedule variance** SV = EV - PV. Negative means behind.
- **Cost variance** CV = EV - AC. Negative means over budget for the work done.
- **Schedule performance index** SPI = EV / PV. Below 1 means behind.
- **Cost performance index** CPI = EV / AC. Below 1 means you are getting less than a naira of work for each naira spent.
- **Estimate at completion** EAC = BAC / CPI, where BAC is the original budget at completion. This assumes that your cost performance so far continues.

:::example title=Reading the numbers on a website project (invented)
A web project has a total budget (BAC) of **₦500,000**. At the end of week 4, the plan says half the work should be finished. The team says it has finished 40 percent of the work. It has spent ₦260,000.

- PV = 50 percent of 500,000 = **₦250,000**
- EV = 40 percent of 500,000 = **₦200,000**
- AC = **₦260,000**

Variances:

- SV = 200,000 - 250,000 = **-₦50,000** (behind schedule)
- CV = 200,000 - 260,000 = **-₦60,000** (over budget)

Indexes:

- SPI = 200,000 / 250,000 = **0.80**. The team has done 80 kobo of work for each naira planned.
- CPI = 200,000 / 260,000 = **0.77** (rounded). Each naira spent has produced about 77 kobo of planned work.

Forecast:

- EAC = 500,000 / 0.769 = about **₦650,000**. If the team keeps performing this way, the project will end around ₦150,000 over budget.

What a manager does with this: it is not a verdict, it is a question. Why is the team behind and over? Rework? Wrong estimates? Waiting for client content? If the cause was a one-off event, such as a week lost to a power problem, the forecast may be too gloomy. If the cause is structural, such as estimates that are consistently low, the forecast is a warning to tell the sponsor now, with options: reduce scope, add money, or move the date.
:::

:::check q13-1
:::

:::figure
type: bars
title: Planned, earned and actual on the website project (invented)
caption: At week 4 the plan called for 250,000 naira of work, the team has completed 200,000 naira worth, and it has spent 260,000. Earned value below both planned value and actual cost means behind schedule and over budget.
unit: naira
- Planned value | 250000
- ! Earned value | 200000
- Actual cost | 260000
:::

EVM works best when the budget is split by work package (so you can credit finished work), the team records time and costs regularly, and the plan is reasonably firm. For small, informal projects you can use it in a simplified way: percent of work finished compared with percent of budget spent.

## Change is normal: control it

Every project gets change requests: "Can we add a feature?", "The client wants a different colour", "The date must move". You cannot refuse all change, and you cannot accept all of it. **Scope creep** is the slow growth of a project through small, unapproved additions. Each addition seems minor, and together they sink the budget and the date.

A simple **change control process**:

:::figure
type: flow
title: Handling a change request
caption: Every change is written down, its effects on scope, time and cost are worked out, the right person decides, and then the plan and baseline are updated and communicated.
- Request | Write it down: who, what, why
- Assess | Effect on scope, time, cost, risk
- Decide | The accountable person approves, rejects or defers
- Update | Change the plan and baseline
- Tell | Inform everyone affected
:::

1. **Capture** each request in writing, with who asked and why.
2. **Assess** the effect on scope, schedule, budget, quality and risk. Involve the people who will do the work.
3. **Decide.** Who has the authority? Small changes within agreed limits might be the manager's decision. Larger ones go to the sponsor. Write down who decides at the start.
4. **Update** the plan, the baseline and the budget if approved.
5. **Communicate** to anyone affected.

Keep a **change log**: number, date, requester, description, impact, decision.

:::compare
weak: "Sure, we can add that. It should not take long."
strong: "That is a good idea. I will check what it needs. Adding a second language version would take about 3 more days and ₦80,000. Do you want me to send a formal change request so you can approve it?"
note: Saying yes or no on the spot is rarely right. The strong reply neither refuses nor accepts blindly. It turns the wish into a decision with numbers.
:::

Not every change is a problem. In agile projects (Lesson 11), the backlog is reordered all the time as learning arrives. The difference is that a team reprioritises within a fixed time and budget limit. If something new comes in, something else comes out or the limit changes by agreement.

## Issues, actions and corrective steps

When a risk occurs (Lesson 9) or a problem appears, record it in an **issue log**: description, impact, owner, action, due date and status. Do not let issues live only in conversation.

When tracking shows you are off plan, you have four main choices:

1. **Recover:** work extra hours, add resources (watch for Brooks's observation from Lesson 6 that adding people can slow a late project), or fix the root cause.
2. **Re-plan:** change the sequence to recover time, such as fast tracking from Lesson 7.
3. **Re-scope:** remove or postpone lower-value work.
4. **Re-baseline:** change the date or budget, with the sponsor's agreement.

Pick the one that suits the cause, tell the sponsor early, and bring options, not just the bad news.

:::keyidea
Measure progress with completed work and remaining effort rather than feelings, compare with a saved baseline using planned, earned and actual values, and put every change through a written assess-and-decide process.
:::

## What you can do now

You can set a baseline, measure progress in ways that resist wishful thinking, calculate and interpret earned value, and control changes. In Lesson 14 you will deal with the people side of trouble: conflict, difficult stakeholders and negotiation.

:::exercise title=Run an earned value check
1. Take a project with a total budget and a plan, real or invented. Choose a date about halfway through.
2. Work out PV from the plan, EV from the work actually completed, and AC from the money actually spent.
3. Calculate SV, CV, SPI, CPI and EAC. Check your arithmetic by multiplying back (for example, CPI x AC should equal EV).
4. Write two sentences for the sponsor: what the numbers say, and what you propose.
5. Write a change request for one real or imagined addition. Fill in its impact on scope, time and cost, and decide who approves it.

A good answer shows the formulas, the arithmetic, and a recommendation that fits the numbers.
:::

lessons.title: Conflict, pressure and negotiation
lessons.subtitle: Every project hits a hard conversation. Learn to find what people really need, say no without damage, and escalate at the right time.
outcomes: Name the five common ways people handle conflict and when each fits
Negotiate on interests instead of positions
Say no or not yet with options, and know when to escalate
lessons.body:
On the 3rd of the month, two weeks before a planned launch on the 17th, the sponsor, a regional manager called Mr Danjuma, calls Funke, the project manager. "The board meets on the 12th, not the 17th. I told them it would be ready. Move the date." Funke's schedule has no float. She has three honest replies available. She can say "Yes, we will find a way," which feels loyal and will break the team. She can say "That is impossible," which feels honest and will end the conversation. Or she can do the harder thing: find out what he needs and bring choices. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

Every project meets pressure from above, disagreement from the side and friction below. Handling it well is part of the job, not a distraction from it.

## Where conflict comes from

Conflict is not a sign that something is wrong with the people. Common sources are all built into projects:

- **Limited resources.** Two projects want the same developer, or two teams want the same budget.
- **Unclear roles.** Both people think they are accountable (Lesson 10).
- **Different goals.** Sales wants it fast, quality wants it right, finance wants it cheap.
- **Schedule pressure.** Tired people are short with each other.
- **Communication gaps.** One person assumed, the other did not know.
- **Personality and style.** One is blunt, one is careful. Neither is wrong.

Most of these are problems with the structure, not people. If you fix the roles, the goals or the information, the heat often drops.

## Five ways people handle conflict

Kenneth Thomas and Ralph Kilmann described five common styles (some books use other names, such as forcing, problem solving and smoothing) in a conflict model they developed in the 1970s. Each style balances two things: how much you push for your own goals and how much you care about the other person's.

- **Competing.** You push your view. Use it when there is an emergency, a safety issue, or a decision that must be made fast and you are accountable. Overused, it breeds resentment.
- **Collaborating.** You work with the other person to find a solution that serves both sets of needs. Best for important issues where both sides' concerns matter and there is time. It takes effort.
- **Compromising.** Each side gives something up. Useful when time is short and a decent solution is fine. It can leave both sides a little unhappy.
- **Avoiding.** You step back or delay. Useful when the issue is trivial, or when emotions need time to cool. Harmful if the problem is important and keeps growing.
- **Accommodating.** You yield. Useful when the issue matters far more to the other person, or when you are wrong. Overused, you become a doormat and your needs vanish.

No style is "best". A good manager can choose among them. A common mistake is using one style for everything, especially avoiding.

:::check q14-1
:::

## Negotiate on interests, not positions

In their classic book *Getting to Yes* (1981), Roger Fisher and William Ury describe principled negotiation. Four ideas carry most of the value:

1. **Separate the people from the problem.** Be soft on the person and hard on the issue. "You always miss deadlines" attacks a person. "The design was due Tuesday and it is Thursday, so what is blocking it?" tackles the problem.
2. **Focus on interests, not positions.** A **position** is what someone says they want ("Move the date to the 12th"). An **interest** is why they want it ("I told the board it would be ready and I do not want to look unreliable"). Positions often clash while interests can often be met in several ways.
3. **Invent options for mutual gain.** Before deciding, brainstorm choices that could satisfy both sides.
4. **Use objective criteria.** Agree on fair standards, such as market rates, past data, or the plan's numbers, instead of a contest of wills.

A fifth, practical idea from the same book is to know your **BATNA**, your best alternative to a negotiated agreement. If talks fail, what will you do? The stronger your alternative, the less you need to give in. And think about theirs too.

:::example title=Funke and the early deadline (invented)
**Step 1: Ask about the interest.** Funke says, "I want to help you with the board. What do you need to show them on the 12th?" Mr Danjuma says the board wants to see the customer portal working and approve the budget for the next phase.

**Step 2: Check the facts.** She shows the critical path. Full launch needs 14 days. Today is the 3rd, so the 12th is 9 days away. Compressing by 5 days would need either more people on the critical activities, which she estimates at ₦300,000 extra with a risk that quality drops, or removing features.

**Step 3: Bring options.**

- **Option A:** Keep the 17th for full launch. On the 12th, present a working demonstration of login and ordering, which are finished by day 8, with the remaining features dated clearly.
- **Option B:** Launch the reduced scope (login, ordering, no reports) on the 12th, and the rest by the 17th, at no extra cost.
- **Option C:** Full launch on the 12th, for an extra ₦300,000 and a higher risk of defects. She recommends against it.

**Step 4: Agree.** Mr Danjuma chooses Option B. His interest, a board that sees a real working system and an approved next phase, is met. Her team keeps a realistic plan. Nobody had to lose face.

Notice the sequence: ask why, show facts, offer choices, let the accountable person decide.
:::

## Saying no, or "not yet"

A project manager who never says no ends up saying a quiet, damaging no later, when the project fails. Practical ways to say it well:

- **Say no to the request, yes to the need.** "I cannot add this by Friday. What I can do is include it in the next phase, or swap it for the report feature. Which do you prefer?"
- **Show the trade-off, not the reluctance.** Use the four limits from Lesson 1. "If we add it, here is the effect on time and cost."
- **Use numbers from the plan.** "The critical path has no float" is harder to argue with than "we are very busy".
- **Offer a date for when you will answer.** "I will check with the team and tell you by 3 pm" is acceptable. A silent delay is not.

:::compare
weak: "That is not possible. We are already behind."
strong: "I want to hit that date. As things stand, the plan finishes on the 17th. To reach the 12th we would have to drop the reporting feature or add ₦300,000. Which would you rather?"
note: The strong reply starts from the shared goal and ends with a choice for the person who has the authority.
:::

## Difficult people

Three common situations:

- **The sponsor who changes their mind.** Keep the charter and change log (Lessons 3 and 13). When a change comes, show the impact and ask for a decision. Do not absorb the cost silently.
- **The team member who is underperforming.** Speak privately, soon, and specifically. Describe what you saw, ask what is getting in the way, agree on one clear next step and a time to check. Many problems are about unclear expectations, workload or personal difficulty. If it continues, involve their line manager.
- **Two people in open conflict.** Meet each separately first, to listen. Then bring them together around the shared goal, ask each to say what they need, and agree on a working rule. Do not take sides in public.

## When to escalate

**Escalation** means taking a problem to someone with more authority. It is not failure. It is a tool. Escalate when:

- The issue is outside your authority (budget, contracts, priorities between projects).
- You have tried reasonable steps and are still stuck.
- A delay would harm the critical path, safety, legal compliance or the client.
- Someone is acting in a way that is unethical or unsafe.

When you do, state the problem, the effect, what you tried, the options and your recommendation. Tell the people involved first, whenever you can, so they are not surprised.

:::keyidea
When tension rises, find out what each person needs, show the facts from the plan, offer options, and let the person with authority choose, using no, yes-if or not-yet instead of a silent maybe.
:::

## What you can do now

You can name your own conflict style and choose others on purpose, negotiate by interests, say no with options, and decide when to escalate. That completes the module on leading and delivering. In Module 4 you will learn to close projects well, choose tools, think about your career, and then build a full project plan as your capstone.

:::exercise title=Rehearse a hard conversation
1. Write down a real or realistic conflict: a deadline moved up, a teammate not delivering, a client demanding extra work.
2. Write the other person's position and then your best guess at their interest. If you can, ask them.
3. List three options that could meet both your interests.
4. Write your opening line using "I want to... and the plan shows... which would you prefer?"
5. Practise it aloud with a friend, or record yourself. Listen for blame words and replace them with facts.
6. Hold the real conversation within a week. Write down what happened and what you would do differently.

A good answer identifies an interest behind the position and offers at least two options.
:::

lessons.title: Quality, handover and closing well
lessons.subtitle: A project is not finished when the work stops. It is finished when the result is accepted, the books are closed and the lessons are saved.
outcomes: Plan quality in from the start instead of inspecting it in at the end
Run a clean acceptance and handover
Hold a lessons-learned review that changes what you do next time
lessons.body:
A company in Port Harcourt delivers an inventory system on the agreed date. The team celebrates and scatters to other work. Six weeks later the client calls: staff cannot find how to run the monthly report, nobody trained the storekeeper, and the supplier's last invoice is still unpaid. The project was "finished" in the plan and unfinished in reality. The team had stopped at delivery and skipped closing. *(Invented story, for illustration.)*

Closing is not paperwork at the end. It is the stage where a project becomes a result someone can actually use, and where the people who did the work get the benefit of what they learned.

## Quality: build it in, do not inspect it in

**Quality** means the result meets the needs and standards you agreed on, not that it is fancy. A quality failure is when the result does not do what was promised or does not work well enough to be used.

Two ideas separate good from poor quality management.

- **Quality assurance** is about the process: doing things so that quality is likely. Clear requirements, checklists, peer review, testing early.
- **Quality control** is about the product: inspecting and testing the result to see whether it meets the standard.

You need both, but assurance is cheaper. Fixing a mistake caught in the plan costs a conversation. Fixing the same mistake after delivery costs rework, money and trust.

Practical ways to build quality in:

1. **Write acceptance criteria early** (Lesson 3). If you know what "pass" means before you start, the team aims at it.
2. **Define "done"** for every work package and for the whole result (Lessons 5 and 11).
3. **Review as you go.** Peer checks, drafts shown to users, a test after each part, not one big test at the end.
4. **Use checklists** for repeatable steps. A good checklist catches common slips that tired people miss.
5. **Test with real users**, not only with the team that built it. The people who made it know too much to see its problems.
6. **Track defects.** Keep a simple list of what was found, how, and what caused it. Patterns point to causes.

Never trade quality away silently when time is short. If you must cut, cut scope openly (Lessons 1 and 13) rather than shipping work that does not meet the agreed standard and hoping nobody notices.

:::check q15-1
:::

## Acceptance and handover

**Acceptance** is the moment the sponsor or client agrees the result meets the agreed criteria. It should be a check against a list, not a mood. A simple process:

1. **Final testing and review** against the acceptance criteria from the charter.
2. **A written list of any remaining defects**, with agreed fix dates or agreed exceptions.
3. **Formal sign-off.** A signature, or at minimum an email that says "accepted". Without written acceptance, there is no clear record that the work was accepted, so it is unclear whether the project is finished and a client may later dispute the result. Check what your contract says.
4. **Handover** to the people who will use and maintain the result. Provide what they need, which usually includes instructions, training, spare parts or access details, contact points for support, and a list of known limits.

Handover is the step people most often skimp. For the inventory system, the handover pack should have included a one-page guide for each monthly task, a training session with the storekeeper and finance staff, a support contact, and the login details transferred to the client's own account, not the developer's.

If the result will be operated by a team that was not part of the project, bring them in early. People accept and use what they helped shape.

## Close the business side

Before the team is released, tie up the loose ends.

- **Contracts and suppliers:** confirm all work was delivered and accepted, and that final payments are made or scheduled. Close or hand on contracts.
- **Finance:** reconcile actual costs against the budget, and record the final figures. Return unused money as agreed.
- **Records:** store the final plan, decision log, change log, risk register and key emails in a shared place the organisation can find later.
- **Resources:** return borrowed equipment, close accounts, stop subscriptions you no longer need.
- **Benefits:** write down how and when you will check that the project achieved its purpose. A project that delivers on time but never improves what it was meant to improve is still a failure. Put a date in the calendar, such as three months after handover, to check the real result.

## People: release them well

Teams that finish a hard project often feel a mix of relief and loss. Treat the end of the project (the Adjourning stage from Lesson 10) as part of the job.

- **Recognise contributions specifically.** "Seun solved the payment failures in three days, which saved the launch" lands better than "great job, team".
- **Give honest feedback** and tell people's line managers what they achieved.
- **Help people move on.** Make sure they know what they are doing next.
- **Say thank you in a visible way.** A small celebration is not wasteful. It is part of building a team that will work for you again.

## Lessons learned

A **lessons-learned review**, also called a retrospective or post-project review, is the habit that makes your next project better than this one. Do it within a few weeks of finishing, while memories are fresh, and with the team in the room.

Keep it blame-free. The aim is to improve the system, not to find a culprit. Four simple questions work:

1. What went well, and should we repeat it?
2. What went badly or surprised us?
3. Why? (Ask "why" more than once to reach the cause.)
4. What will we do differently next time? (Each answer becomes an action with an owner.)

:::example title=A short lessons-learned record (invented, inventory project)
**What went well:** Weekly demonstrations to the client caught two misunderstandings in week 3. The risk register flagged the supplier delay early, and the second supplier was ready.

**What went badly:** Training was planned for the last week and squeezed out by testing delays. The final invoice was not scheduled in the cash plan.

**Why:** Training had no owner and was not in the schedule as a critical activity. The cash plan was built from the budget, not the contract's payment terms.

**Do differently:**
1. Put training and handover in the WBS as work packages with owners from the start. (Owner: project manager, next project)
2. Build the cash flow plan from contract payment dates. (Owner: finance lead, now)
3. Keep the weekly demonstration habit. (Owner: team)

**Where saved:** Shared folder "Projects", file "Lessons learned register", plus a short note emailed to the department head.
:::

A review that ends in a document no one reads has failed. Put the actions into your next project's plan, and keep a **lessons-learned register** that you check at the start of every new project. Your best estimates (Lesson 6) will come from these records.

:::compare
weak: "We finished. Thanks everyone. Let's move on to the next one."
strong: "The result was accepted in writing on Friday. The handover pack and training are done, final invoices are scheduled, and the team is meeting on Tuesday for a one-hour review. In three months I will check whether the monthly report time has fallen as planned."
note: The strong version names acceptance, handover, money, learning and a later check of the benefit.
:::

:::keyidea
Close a project on purpose: build quality in from the start, get written acceptance, hand over with training, settle contracts and money, thank the team, and record lessons that change your next plan.
:::

## What you can do now

You can plan quality, run acceptance and handover, close the finances and contracts, release the team well, and hold a review that leads to change. In Lesson 16 you will choose practical tools and look at how this knowledge can become work or a career. In Lesson 17 you will put everything together in a capstone plan.

:::exercise title=Write a closing checklist and a review
1. Think of a project you have completed, such as an event, a job, a school project or a purchase. Choose one where the end felt messy.
2. Write what a proper close would have included: acceptance, handover, money, records, thanks, benefit check.
3. Write a lessons-learned record with the four questions above. Include at least three actions with owners.
4. Choose one action and put it into a real plan or calendar this week.

A good answer has at least one lesson that identifies a root cause, not just a symptom.
:::

lessons.title: Tools, templates and turning the skill into work
lessons.subtitle: You do not need expensive software. You need a small set of simple tools, good habits and proof that you can deliver.
outcomes: Choose a simple, low-cost tool set for planning and tracking
Build a personal template pack you can reuse
Describe realistic paths to use project management in a job or freelance work
lessons.body:
A common beginner mistake is to spend a week choosing software and no time managing anything. A project run on paper and a spreadsheet by someone who understands scope, risk and communication beats a project run on an expensive tool by someone who does not. Tools help you do the thinking faster and share it. They do not do the thinking.

## A simple tool set

Think in jobs, not brands. A small project needs six jobs done.

| Job | Free or low-cost options | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Task board | A wall of sticky notes, Trello, or a spreadsheet with columns | Good for Kanban (Lesson 11) |
| Schedule and Gantt chart | A spreadsheet, or GanttProject | GanttProject is a free desktop program that draws Gantt charts and handles dependencies |
| Budget and cost tracking | Google Sheets or Excel | Keep one sheet with budget, actual and variance columns |
| Risk register and logs | A shared spreadsheet | Risk, issue, change and decision logs all work as simple tables |
| Documents and notes | Google Docs, a notes app, or a shared folder | One agreed place for the charter, plan and decisions |
| Communication | WhatsApp, email, a call app | Agree rules from Lesson 12 |

Tool features, free plan limits and prices change often. Before you pick one, open its pricing or help page and check what the current free plan allows, such as how many boards, people or files. Do not rely on what you read in an old article, including this one.

How to choose among tools:

1. **Start with the team.** The best tool is the one everyone will actually open. If the team lives in WhatsApp, a board that nobody visits will fail.
2. **Prefer simple.** Each extra field and feature is something someone must keep updated.
3. **Check it works on a phone and offline.** In many places connectivity is unreliable. A tool that needs a perfect connection will be abandoned.
4. **Keep your data portable.** Choose tools where you can export your data in a common format such as a spreadsheet, so you are not trapped.
5. **Do not mix too many.** Three tools that everyone uses beat ten that nobody does.

## A spreadsheet is a project management tool

You can run a small project with one spreadsheet that has these tabs: **Charter** (the one-page summary), **WBS and schedule** (tasks, owner, duration, start, finish, predecessor, status), **Budget** (planned, actual, variance), **Risks** (the register from Lesson 9), **Decisions and changes** (the logs), and **Status** (the update you send each week). Simple formulas do much of the work: totals for budget, variance as planned minus actual, and finish date as start plus duration.

:::example title=The schedule tab in a spreadsheet (invented)
A small shop move tracked in one sheet. Columns: ID, task, owner, duration in days, start day, finish day, predecessor, status.

| ID | Task | Owner | Days | Start | Finish | Predecessor | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Sign lease for new shop | Chuka | 2 | 0 | 2 | none | Done |
| 2 | Order shelving | Chuka | 5 | 2 | 7 | 1 | Doing |
| 3 | Paint and wire shop | Ibrahim | 6 | 2 | 8 | 1 | Doing |
| 4 | Fit shelving | Ibrahim | 2 | 8 | 10 | 2, 3 | To do |
| 5 | Move stock and reopen | Team | 2 | 10 | 12 | 4 | To do |

The finish column is just start plus days (for example, row 4 is 8 + 2 = 10). Each start is the latest finish among its predecessors: task 4 waits for both 2 (finish 7) and 3 (finish 8), so it starts at 8. Painting is therefore on the critical path and ordering shelving has 1 day of float. A sheet this size does the same thinking as a Gantt chart, and anyone with a phone can read it.
:::

## Build your own template pack

Over time, collect the documents you reuse so you never start from a blank page. A good personal pack has:

1. **Project charter** (one page)
2. **Stakeholder list and communication plan**
3. **WBS and activity list**
4. **Schedule or Gantt**
5. **Budget with contingency**
6. **Risk register**
7. **RACI chart**
8. **Weekly status update**
9. **Change request and change log**
10. **Lessons-learned record**

You will build most of these in the capstone in Lesson 17. Keep them in a folder with a clear name. Improve them after every project.

:::check q16-1
:::

## Using the skill in work

Project management is not only a job title. It is a way to do work. Here are realistic paths.

**Inside your current job or study.** Volunteer to organise the next event, report, launch or office move. Use the charter, WBS, risk list and status update. Document what you did. This is the easiest way to build real experience without changing jobs, and it makes your work visible.

**Project coordinator and assistant roles.** Many organisations hire people to support project managers by keeping schedules, taking notes, chasing updates and preparing reports. Roles carry titles such as project coordinator, project assistant or project administrator, though the names vary. Read job advertisements to see what the employers around you ask for and compare them with your skills.

**Freelance and small-business projects.** Small businesses, churches, schools, NGOs and online sellers often have projects (a launch, a move, an event, a website, a migration) and no one to run them. A clear scope, plan and regular updates is a service people pay for. The scoping and pricing habits from Lessons 3 and 8 protect you. Start by running one project for someone you know, for a low fee or free, in exchange for a written testimonial and permission to describe the result in your portfolio. Be honest about your experience and let the project show it.

**Combining with another skill.** Project management multiplies other skills. A designer who can run the whole project is more valuable than one who only designs. The same goes for writers, developers, builders and marketers.

## Certifications: what exists and what to check

Some employers value formal credentials. The main ones are run by organisations whose rules change, so always read the current official page before you spend money. As checked on 24 October 2026:

- **CAPM (Certified Associate in Project Management)** from PMI is aimed at people starting out. PMI's page lists eligibility as a secondary-level education, being at least 18, and at least 23 hours of project management education before the exam. It states no experience is required.
- **PMP (Project Management Professional)** from PMI is for people with experience leading projects. PMI launched an updated PMP exam in July 2026 that places more weight on business environment and covers topics such as AI and sustainability. Its page says applicants need 35 hours of project management training, and that from 1 December 2026 live training hours must come from certain approved providers. For the education and experience requirements, check PMI's application page.
- **PRINCE2** is another widely used method, especially in public and international organisations. Its qualification structure and training providers are separate from PMI's.
- **Agile and Scrum certificates** are offered by several organisations, including Scrum.org and Scrum Alliance. They differ in content, cost and recognition.

Important honesty points. This course is **not** PMI-authorised training and **does not count** toward the training hours that PMI requires. It does teach the ideas that these certifications test, but the courses, exams and fees are separate. A certificate is not required to start doing project work, and many people build a record through real projects first. Exam fees and rules change, and exchange rates affect the cost in naira, so check the cost before you plan. Be wary of anyone who promises a guaranteed job from a certificate.

## Keep learning

Read the primary sources listed in this course's sources page: the Scrum Guide, the Kanban Guide, and PMI's published material. Practise on real projects. Join a local project management or agile community, in person or online. Ask people to review your plans. And keep your lessons-learned register.

:::keyidea
Choose the simplest tools your team will really use, build a reusable template pack, and prove your skill through real, documented projects before or alongside any certificate.
:::

## What you can do now

You can choose simple tools, assemble a template pack, find realistic ways to use the skill, and read certification information critically. In Lesson 17 you will put everything together in a capstone: a complete project plan for a real project.

:::exercise title=Assemble your template pack
1. Create a folder called "PM templates".
2. In a spreadsheet, create the tabs listed above: Charter, WBS and schedule, Budget, Risks, Decisions and changes, Status.
3. Add column headings from the lessons. For example, the risk register needs ID, risk, likelihood, impact, expected cost, response, trigger and owner.
4. Add one example row to each tab from a real or imagined project.
5. Write a one-page document that explains in plain words how you will use these tabs each week.
6. Open the official page for one certification that interests you. Write down the current requirements and cost, and the date you checked.

A good answer is a spreadsheet someone else could pick up and use without asking you questions.
:::

lessons.title: Capstone: plan a real project from start to finish
lessons.subtitle: Bring every skill together in one complete project plan you can show to a sponsor, a client or an employer.
outcomes: Produce a complete project plan using the full set of course tools
Check your own plan against a quality rubric
Present the plan in a short, clear briefing
lessons.body:
You now have the full set of tools: a charter, a stakeholder map, a work breakdown, honest estimates, a schedule with a critical path, a budget with contingency, a risk register, a team structure, a way to track progress and control change, and a plan to close. A skill is proven when you use it on something real. This capstone asks you to do that, and to end with a plan you could hand to someone and say, "This is how I would run it."

## Choose the right project

Pick a project that is real, small enough to plan in a few days of effort, and meaningful to you. Good choices:

- A community or school event (a fair, a clean-up, a training day).
- A small business launch or change (a new product, a delivery service, a shop move).
- A personal project with real stakes (a house move, a wedding, a certification plan, a side income project).
- A volunteer or church project (a building repair, an outreach, a fundraising drive).
- A work project you are allowed to plan.

Avoid projects that are too vague ("grow my business"), too large ("build a hospital"), or entirely outside your control. If you can, choose one you will really run. Real plans meet real surprises, and that is where you learn most.

## The capstone deliverables

Your capstone is a single plan, in a document or spreadsheet, with ten parts. Each part matches a lesson, so you can look back for guidance.

| Part | What it contains | Lesson |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Charter | Purpose, goal with numbers and dates, scope in and out, success criteria, assumptions, constraints, key dates, budget ceiling, people | 3 |
| 2. Method | Predictive, agile or hybrid, with a reason using the four questions | 2 |
| 3. Stakeholders | List, power and interest grid, communication plan | 4 |
| 4. WBS | A breakdown to work packages with owners and a definition of done | 5 |
| 5. Estimates | Three-point estimates for the main activities, stated as ranges | 6 |
| 6. Schedule | Dependencies, critical path, float and a Gantt chart or timeline | 7 |
| 7. Budget and people | Bottom-up budget with contingency, cash flow note, check for overload | 8 |
| 8. Risks | At least ten risks, with the top five ranked and with responses, triggers and owners | 9 |
| 9. Team and control | RACI, how you will track progress, change control process, status update format | 10, 12, 13 |
| 10. Close | Acceptance criteria, handover plan, lessons-learned plan, benefit check date | 15 |

## A suggested order of work

1. **Day 1: Define.** Charter, method, stakeholders. Talk to at least one real stakeholder before you finish.
2. **Day 2: Break down and estimate.** WBS, activities, three-point estimates.
3. **Day 3: Schedule and price.** Dependencies, critical path, Gantt, budget, contingency.
4. **Day 4: Risks and team.** Pre-mortem, register, RACI, tracking and change control.
5. **Day 5: Close and review.** Closing plan, then read everything as if you were the sponsor and fix gaps.
6. **Day 6: Present.** Write a one-page summary and practise a five-minute briefing.

Do not try to make it perfect the first time. A plan is a working document that improves when you test it against people and facts.

:::example title=A compact specimen plan (invented project)
This shortened example shows the shape. Your plan will be longer.

**Project:** Community clean-up and recycling day at Unity Market, Ilorin.
**1. Charter.** Goal: on 18 April, 80 volunteers collect and sort waste from the market and its drains, and the market association agrees a weekly collection plan. Budget ceiling ₦450,000. Out of scope: building new drains, buying a skip truck. Success criteria: at least 60 volunteers present; at least 5 tonnes collected and sorted (to be measured by weighing at the dump); written weekly collection plan signed by the association chair by 30 April.
**2. Method.** Predictive: the date is fixed, permits are needed, change is costly.
**3. Stakeholders.** Manage closely: market association chair, local government environment officer. Keep satisfied: the market's landlord. Keep informed: traders, volunteers, neighbours.
**4. WBS (top level).** Permits and agreements; volunteers recruited and briefed; equipment and safety supplies; waste transport and disposal; publicity; event day; follow-up plan.
**5 and 6. Schedule.** Permit: expected 11 working days by the PERT formula (optimistic 6, most likely 10, pessimistic 20, spread about 2.3), and it is on the critical path with transport booking. Float on publicity is 8 days.
**7. Budget.** Gloves and bags ₦120,000; transport ₦140,000; refreshments ₦90,000; publicity ₦30,000; sub-total ₦380,000; contingency ₦70,000 (about 18 percent of the subtotal, because the permit and weather are uncertain); total ₦450,000. Check: 120 + 140 + 90 + 30 = 380; 380 + 70 = 450.
**8. Top risks.** Permit delay (30 percent, mitigate by applying today and naming a backup date); rain (25 percent, accept with a rain date); too few volunteers (30 percent, mitigate through school and church groups).
**9. Control.** RACI with the association chair accountable for permits. Weekly update by WhatsApp voice note plus a one-page summary. Any change over ₦20,000 goes to the chair.
**10. Close.** Acceptance: chair signs the collection plan. Review meeting two weeks after. Benefit check: market cleanliness inspected after two months.
:::

:::check q17-1
:::

## Quality rubric: check your own plan

Score each line yes, partly or no. Fix every "no" before you present.

1. The goal contains numbers and dates, and a stranger could check it.
2. The scope says what is out as well as what is in.
3. Every stakeholder who could stop the project is on the list, and you have a plan for each.
4. Every work package has one owner and a definition of done.
5. Estimates are ranges, and you can say where they came from.
6. You know your critical path and the float of at least the main activities.
7. The budget has a visible contingency, and the arithmetic adds up (check it twice).
8. At least ten risks are listed, the top five have responses, triggers and owners.
9. There is a rule for how changes are approved and who decides.
10. The closing plan includes handover, finance, lessons learned and a date to check the benefit.
11. Every number is either real, sourced, or clearly marked as an estimate or an assumption.
12. Another person could pick up the plan and run the project without asking you what you meant.

## Present your plan

A plan that is not communicated helps nobody. Prepare a **five-minute briefing** with these parts:

1. **The problem and goal** (30 seconds).
2. **What we will deliver, and what we will not** (30 seconds).
3. **The plan on one page:** milestones, critical path, budget total with contingency (90 seconds).
4. **The three biggest risks and what you will do** (60 seconds).
5. **What you need from the audience now**, such as approval, money, people or a decision (60 seconds).
6. **Questions** (the rest).

End with the specific ask. A briefing without a request is just a talk.

:::compare
weak: "This plan is quite detailed. There are many parts. I hope it will go well."
strong: "The project delivers a clean market by 18 April for ₦450,000, including ₦70,000 contingency. The critical path is the permit, so I need your signature on the application by Friday. The biggest risk is a permit delay, and my backup is a second date on 25 April."
note: The strong briefing is specific, honest about risk, and finishes with a request.
:::

:::keyidea
A good plan is clear enough that someone else could run the project from it, honest about uncertainty, and finished only when you have tested it with real people and real numbers.
:::

## After the capstone

If you can, run the project. Track real progress against your plan, record what changes, and close with a lessons-learned review. Then keep the plan, your status updates and your review as evidence of what you can do. Show them to a manager, a client, or an interviewer. Evidence of a real plan and a real result is worth more than any claim of "good organisation skills".

## What you can do now

You can plan a real project from first idea to closure, check it against a rubric, and present it with a clear request. You have the main tools a working project manager uses. The next step is to use them, make mistakes while the stakes are small, and keep a record of what you learn.

:::exercise title=Complete your capstone
1. Choose your project using the guidance above and write one sentence on why it is a good choice.
2. Produce all ten parts of the plan, in a document or in the spreadsheet template pack from Lesson 16.
3. Run the 12-point rubric. List every "no" or "partly" and fix it.
4. Show the plan to one person, ideally someone who would be affected by the project, and ask them to find the weakest part. Improve it.
5. Write and practise your five-minute briefing. Deliver it to a real person, or record yourself and listen back.
6. Write three sentences: what you are most proud of, what was hardest, and what you would do differently next time.

A good capstone is one a sponsor could approve, because the goal is clear, the plan is believable, the risks are honest and the ask is specific.
:::

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a project rather than ongoing work?

options.text: Serving customers at a restaurant every evening
Running payroll at the end of each month
Opening a second pharmacy branch by a fixed date
Answering the same customer questions each day

quiz.explanation: A project is temporary and creates something new. Opening a branch has an end and produces a new result. The other options repeat the same process with no planned end.

quiz.prompt: A client asks you to finish a month earlier with the same budget and the same scope. According to the lesson, what is the best first response?

options.text: Agree and work longer hours to protect the budget
Refuse, because the original plan cannot change
Say you will try and see how it goes
Show the trade-off and offer choices, such as more money or less scope

quiz.explanation: The four limits are linked, so one cannot move alone. Making the trade-off visible lets the decision-maker choose. Silent agreement or flat refusal hides the problem.

quiz.prompt: Which pair describes the two kinds of project success the lesson separates?
quiz.explanation: Delivery success asks whether you finished within the agreed limits. Result success asks whether what you made solves the real problem. A project can pass the first and fail the second.

quiz.prompt: What does the lesson say about Flyvbjerg's finding that only about 8.5 percent of projects met their original cost and time estimates?

options.text: It proves every project over a month long will fail
It applies only to building projects
It leans toward large projects, but shows that finishing exactly as first planned is the exception
It shows project managers are not needed

quiz.explanation: The database is about 16,000 projects, mostly large ones such as infrastructure and technology. The honest reading is that exact delivery is rare, so good management is about finding surprises early.

quiz.prompt: A school fair plan has 30 stalls, a fixed budget and a fixed date. The head teacher wants an extra day. Which statement is true?

options.text: The extra day changes at least one other limit, such as cost or scope
The extra day is free if the hall is available

quiz.explanation: Scope, time, cost and quality are linked. Adding a day adds hall and supervision cost, or something else must be cut.

quiz.prompt: Which project is the best fit for a predictive (plan-first) approach?

options.text: A student website whose features nobody can predict
Building an auditorium to an approved design where changes after pouring concrete are costly
A new app where users give feedback every week
A blog whose topics change each month

quiz.explanation: Clear requirements and costly change point toward predictive. The other examples have unclear needs and cheap change, which favour agile.

quiz.prompt: Which is one of the four value pairs in the Agile Manifesto?

options.text: Responding to change over following a plan

quiz.explanation: The manifesto says there is value in the items on the right, but the items on the left are valued more. Responding to change over following a plan is one of the four pairs.

quiz.prompt: A team says, "We are agile, so we do not need a plan or a budget." What is wrong with this?

options.text: Agile changes how you plan, not whether you have a goal, a budget limit and a date
Agile requires a longer plan than predictive
Agile teams must always have a fixed price contract

quiz.explanation: Agile plans in short cycles and adapts, but the sponsor still needs a goal, limits and dates they can rely on.
