quiz.prompt: A company launches a new soap. Factory, packaging and date are fixed by contracts, but advertising messages can be tested and changed cheaply. What is the best approach?

options.text: Hybrid, with predictive planning for supply and agile cycles for marketing

quiz.explanation: Hybrid uses each style where it fits. Contracts favour predictive for the factory side, and cheap change favours agile for marketing.

quiz.prompt: Which stage runs alongside planning and execution instead of coming after them?
quiz.explanation: Monitoring and controlling compares progress with the plan the whole time. It is not a final stage.

quiz.prompt: Which goal is the strongest?

options.text: Do a good job on the clinic move
Open on 1 March with all five consulting rooms working, within ₦3,500,000

quiz.explanation: The last goal has a date, a number and a check that a stranger can make. The others cannot be checked.

quiz.prompt: Why is the out-of-scope list so important?

options.text: It protects the project when someone later asks for extras, because you can point to what was agreed
It shows the sponsor what you cannot do

quiz.explanation: Without exclusions, people assume what they want is included. An agreed out-of-scope list is the basis of scope control.

quiz.prompt: What is an assumption in a charter?

options.text: A risk that has already happened
Something you treat as true without proof, which may become a risk if false

quiz.explanation: Assumptions are possible risks. If an assumption turns out false, the plan must change. Constraints are the fixed limits.

quiz.prompt: What is the main purpose of a project charter?

options.text: To formally start the project and record purpose, goals, scope, key limits and who is in charge
To list every task in detail

quiz.explanation: The charter is short. The sponsor agrees to it, which gives the manager authority and gives everyone a document to return to.

quiz.prompt: Which is a result criterion rather than a delivery criterion?

options.text: Every consulting room has working power and water

quiz.explanation: Result criteria describe whether what was made works for its users. Date and budget are delivery criteria.

quiz.prompt: A regulator has a lot of power over your project but little interest in the day-to-day detail. Where do they go on the grid, and what is the approach?

options.text: Keep satisfied, with short updates and no surprises

quiz.explanation: High power and low interest means keep satisfied. Do not overload them, but never let them be surprised.

quiz.prompt: In the Kano market example, why did the project stop?

options.text: The traders' association was never consulted and the block affected their trucks' path

quiz.explanation: The plan itself was good. A stakeholder who could be disturbed was forgotten, which the question "who could be disturbed?" would have caught.

quiz.prompt: Which communication habit does the lesson recommend for bad news?

options.text: Wait until the end of the project
Send it in a long group message
Deliver it early, preferably by voice or in person, with a proposed fix
Let someone else tell the sponsor

quiz.explanation: News does not get better with waiting. A sponsor who hears early can help, but one who hears late can only react.

quiz.prompt: Which question belongs in the first step of finding stakeholders?

options.text: Who could be disturbed or harmed by the result?
Who is the cheapest to ignore?

quiz.explanation: Asking who is disturbed or can stop you reveals the stakeholders most often forgotten.

quiz.prompt: What should a communication plan state for each stakeholder?

options.text: What they need, how often, through which channel and from whom

quiz.explanation: A communication plan is a simple table answering who needs what, how often, by which channel and from whom.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a well-formed work package?

options.text: Announcement published on three channels by 28 March, with one named owner

quiz.explanation: A good work package passes the done test and the owner test. Two people could agree whether it is finished, and one person is responsible.

quiz.prompt: What does the 100 percent rule say?

options.text: Every task must be 100 percent funded
Every team member must work full time
The pieces under a parent must add up to the whole parent, with nothing missing and nothing extra
A project must finish with 100 percent of its budget unspent

quiz.explanation: Missing work becomes a surprise later. Extra work is out of scope and wastes money.

quiz.prompt: Why should the WBS list deliverables rather than only actions?

options.text: Deliverables are easier to check, because you can see whether the thing exists
Actions are not allowed in planning

quiz.explanation: "Menu printed" can be checked. Actions come later as the activity list for each work package.

quiz.prompt: Which is a common WBS mistake?

options.text: Building it with the people who will do the work
Giving management work such as testing and approvals its own boxes
Stopping at "Marketing", which nobody can tell is done or not

quiz.explanation: A box that is too big hides the work and cannot be estimated or owned. The other options are good practice.

quiz.prompt: In the payment set-up example, activity 2 contains waiting time. Why does that matter?

options.text: It means the activity needs no owner
It means the package is out of scope
It adds calendar days without adding effort, so the schedule must account for it

quiz.explanation: Waiting for approval or a provider uses calendar time, not effort. The schedule must show it.

quiz.prompt: What is the planning fallacy?

options.text: Predicting your tasks will take less time than they do, by imagining the smooth path and ignoring past experience
Overestimating how long other people's tasks will take

quiz.explanation: People imagine the best case and ignore how long similar tasks took before. In the 1994 student study, only about 30 percent finished by their best-guess time.

quiz.prompt: Optimistic 2 days, most likely 5 days, pessimistic 14 days. What is the PERT expected time?
What is the PERT spread (standard deviation) for O = 2 and P = 14?
Which is the best way to handle buffers?

options.text: Add hidden padding to every task
Estimate tasks honestly and add visible contingency at project level, managed by the project manager
Let each team member keep their own secret buffer

quiz.explanation: Hidden padding tends to be used up. Visible project-level contingency can be discussed and protected.

quiz.prompt: The project is late. According to Brooks's observation, what usually happens if you add people to a late software project?

options.text: It gets done faster in all cases
It tends to get later, because newcomers need training and communication grows

quiz.explanation: Where work can be divided, extra people can help. Where it cannot, or when training costs are large, adding people can slow the project.

quiz.prompt: What is the critical path?

options.text: The path with the most expensive tasks
The longest chain of dependent activities, which sets the earliest finish date
The tasks the sponsor likes best
The tasks that carry the most risk

quiz.explanation: Any delay on the critical path moves the finish date by the same amount, because it has zero float.

quiz.prompt: In the lesson's network, which activity has 4 days of float?
quiz.explanation: Training needs only the design and is needed only at launch. It can slip 4 days without delaying the project.

quiz.prompt: Approvals in the example network slips from 3 days to 5. What happens to the project finish?

options.text: It moves from 14 to 15 days, because approvals used its 1 day of float and then went 1 day over

quiz.explanation: Build must wait for both approvals and design. Approvals now ends on day 7, one day after design, so the finish moves one day.

quiz.prompt: Which describes "fast tracking"?

options.text: Running activities in parallel that were planned in sequence, accepting more risk of rework

quiz.explanation: Fast tracking overlaps activities. Crashing is adding resources. Both shorten the critical path and carry costs or risks.

quiz.prompt: What is a limit of a basic Gantt chart?

options.text: It may not show dependencies clearly, and its neat bars can suggest more certainty than the estimates have
It always shows the critical path automatically

quiz.explanation: A Gantt chart is a view of the plan. The numbers inside are still estimates.

quiz.prompt: What is the best basis for a reliable project budget?

options.text: A bottom-up estimate built from the work breakdown
A top-down guess from a similar-sounding event
The most the sponsor can pay
Last year's budget with no changes

quiz.explanation: Bottom-up estimating prices each work package, then adds up, which is more reliable than a single top-down guess.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between contingency and management reserve?

options.text: Contingency is for identified or expected risks and is controlled by the project manager. Management reserve is held by the sponsor for unforeseen events
Contingency is held by the sponsor and reserve by the manager

quiz.explanation: Contingency sits inside the project budget. Management reserve needs the sponsor's approval to use.

quiz.prompt: A budget has a subtotal of ₦1,080,000 and a contingency of ₦120,000. Roughly what percentage is the contingency of the subtotal?
quiz.explanation: 120,000 / 1,080,000 is about 0.111, so about 11 percent.

quiz.prompt: As a freelancer on a fixed price contract, what protects you most if your estimate is too low?

options.text: Working longer hours without telling the client
A clear, written scope and a process for priced changes
A lower price than your estimate, to win the work

quiz.explanation: In fixed price work the risk of a low estimate is yours. A clear scope and priced change requests protect you.

quiz.prompt: A person assigned 55 hours of work in one week while having other duties is a sign that...

options.text: The plan is broken, however good the Gantt chart looks
The project is ahead of schedule

quiz.explanation: Resource overload makes the schedule impossible. Move non-critical work into float, add help or move the date.

quiz.prompt: What is the difference between a risk and an issue?

options.text: A risk has already happened. An issue is only possible
A risk is an uncertain event that might happen. An issue is a problem that has already occurred or is certain
Risks are always good and issues always bad

quiz.explanation: When a risk occurs it becomes an issue and moves to the issue log.

quiz.prompt: A risk has a 30 percent chance of costing ₦200,000. What is its expected cost?
quiz.explanation: Probability times impact: 0.30 x 200,000 = 60,000.

quiz.prompt: Which response to a threat reduces the likelihood or impact without removing the risk?
quiz.explanation: Mitigation lowers likelihood or impact, such as ordering cable early. Avoid removes the risk by changing the plan. Transfer moves the financial effect to someone else.

quiz.prompt: What is a pre-mortem?

options.text: A review after the project ends
An exercise where the team imagines the project has already failed and writes down why

quiz.explanation: Imagining failure as real makes people speak more freely about what could go wrong.

quiz.prompt: Which risk statement is most useful?

options.text: Our only cable supplier may reassign our order, causing a three-week delay

quiz.explanation: A useful risk statement is specific about cause, event and effect, and can be given an owner, a trigger and a response.

quiz.prompt: According to Tuckman's model, what is the storming stage?

options.text: A sign that you chose the wrong team and should replace it
The stage when the project ends
A stage when the team works perfectly
A stage of disagreement about roles and methods that is a normal part of development

quiz.explanation: Storming is uncomfortable but normal. Bring conflict into the open and return to the goals. A team that seems to skip it may be hiding its disagreements.

quiz.prompt: In a RACI chart, how many people should be Accountable for one task?
quiz.explanation: One accountable person owns the result and has the final say. Two A's lead each person to assume the other decided.

quiz.prompt: According to Google's Project Aristotle findings, which factor was listed as the most important for team effectiveness?
quiz.explanation: Psychological safety means people feel safe to take risks, ask questions and admit mistakes. It was listed first of five factors.

quiz.prompt: Which is the best way to delegate?

options.text: Say the outcome you need, give authority to match, and agree check-in points
Give detailed steps and check every hour
Hand over tasks without access or decisions

quiz.explanation: Delegating hands over responsibility, which needs authority and clear outcomes. Constant checking and tasks without access both fail.

quiz.prompt: A row in a RACI chart has no R. What does it mean?

options.text: Nobody is assigned to do the work

quiz.explanation: R means responsible for doing the work. A row without R has no one doing it.

quiz.prompt: According to the Scrum Guide, how long can a Sprint be?
quiz.explanation: Sprints are fixed-length events of one month or less to create consistency.

quiz.prompt: Who decides what is most valuable to build next in Scrum?
quiz.explanation: The Product Owner orders the Product Backlog. The Scrum Master helps the team follow Scrum, and the Developers do the work.

quiz.prompt: What is a WIP limit on a Kanban board?

options.text: A cap on how many items can be in a stage at once

quiz.explanation: Limiting work in progress forces finishing before starting and reveals bottlenecks.

quiz.prompt: A studio always has 12 jobs in progress and finishes 3 per week. By Little's Law, what is the average time to finish a job?
quiz.explanation: Average time = work in progress / throughput = 12 / 3 = 4 weeks. Cutting WIP to 6 at the same throughput gives 2 weeks.

quiz.prompt: Which is a warning sign that a team is following Scrum's form but not its purpose?

options.text: The Sprint ends with a review of finished work
The Daily Scrum has become a status report to the boss
The team agrees a Definition of Done

quiz.explanation: The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute event for the Developers to inspect progress and adjust their plan. It is not a report to a manager.

quiz.prompt: What is a good reason to hold a meeting?

options.text: To share information that could be read in two minutes
To make a decision that needs several people's input

quiz.explanation: Meetings are best for deciding, solving problems and aligning. Simple information is quicker to read.

quiz.prompt: What habit catches most misunderstandings at the end of a meeting?

options.text: Reading the actions, owners and dates back aloud

quiz.explanation: A thirty-second read-back confirms who is doing what by when.

quiz.prompt: Which message is most likely to be acted on?

options.text: Following up on that thing, let me know
Need your confirmation by Wednesday 5 pm on banner design A, so printing can start Thursday

quiz.explanation: A good message puts the point first, names the question, the deadline and what happens next.

quiz.prompt: What does an amber status mean in a status update?

options.text: Off track and help is needed now
At risk, with a plan, and you should say why

quiz.explanation: Green is on track, amber is at risk with a plan, red is off track and help is needed. Never use green to avoid worrying people.

quiz.prompt: Why keep a decision log?

options.text: So that weeks later you can answer why a decision was made in seconds

quiz.explanation: A simple log of date, decision, decider and reason prevents lost decisions in chat streams.

quiz.prompt: Planned value is ₦250,000, earned value is ₦200,000 and actual cost is ₦260,000. What is the schedule performance index (SPI)?
quiz.explanation: SPI = EV / PV = 200,000 / 250,000 = 0.80, so the project is behind schedule.

quiz.prompt: Using the same numbers, what is the cost variance (CV)?
quiz.explanation: CV = EV - AC = 200,000 - 260,000 = -60,000, so the project is over budget for the work done.

quiz.prompt: The 90 percent syndrome describes:

options.text: A team that finishes at 90 percent quality
A project that reports being nearly done for weeks because percent complete is a feeling and not a measurement
A project that spends 90 percent of the budget on day one

quiz.explanation: Use measures that are hard to bend, such as done or not done, weighted milestones and remaining effort.

quiz.prompt: What is scope creep?

options.text: A rule that scope must never change
The slow growth of a project through small unapproved additions

quiz.explanation: Each addition seems minor, but together they sink budget and date. A change control process prevents it.

quiz.prompt: A client asks for an extra language version. What is the best reply?

options.text: Say yes, it should not take long
Say you will assess it, then give the time and cost and ask whether to proceed with a formal change request

quiz.explanation: A good reply neither refuses nor accepts blindly. It turns the wish into a decision with numbers.

quiz.prompt: Funke's sponsor demands an earlier date. What is the first step the lesson recommends?

options.text: Ask what he needs, which means finding the interest behind the position

quiz.explanation: The position was "move the date". The interest was a board that sees a working system and approves the next phase. Interests often have several ways to be met.

quiz.prompt: In Fisher and Ury's approach, what is a position?
quiz.explanation: A position is the stated demand. An interest is the reason behind it. The alternative if talks fail is the BATNA.

quiz.prompt: Which conflict style fits a true emergency where you are accountable and a fast decision is needed?
quiz.explanation: Competing, or forcing, fits emergencies and safety issues. It is risky if overused.

quiz.prompt: When is escalation appropriate?

options.text: When the issue is outside your authority, or you have tried reasonable steps and are still stuck
Only at the end of the project

quiz.explanation: Escalation is a tool. State the problem, effect, what you tried, options and your recommendation.

quiz.prompt: Which is the best way to say no to a request?

options.text: Say nothing and hope it goes away
Say no to the request but yes to the need, show the trade-off and offer choices

quiz.explanation: Using numbers from the plan and offering options keeps the shared goal in view and gives the decision to the person with authority.

quiz.prompt: Which statement correctly separates quality assurance from quality control?

options.text: Assurance is about the process that makes good quality likely, and control is inspecting and testing the result
Assurance is inspecting the result, and control is the process
Assurance happens only at the end

quiz.explanation: Assurance builds quality in, which is cheaper. Control checks the product against the standard. You need both.

quiz.prompt: Why is written acceptance important?

options.text: It makes the project look official
It allows the team to skip testing
Without it there is no clear record that the work was accepted, so disputes are harder to settle

quiz.explanation: Acceptance should be a check against agreed criteria, recorded in a signature or an email that says accepted. Check what your contract says about its legal effect.

quiz.prompt: Which question belongs in a blame-free lessons-learned review?

options.text: Why did things go badly, and what will we do differently next time?
Who should be removed from the next project?
How can we hide the problems?

quiz.explanation: The aim is to improve the system. Each answer becomes an action with an owner.

quiz.prompt: What is the best use of a benefit check date, such as three months after handover?

options.text: To confirm the project achieved its purpose in real use

quiz.explanation: A project that delivers on time but does not improve what it was meant to improve is still a failure. A later check shows the real result.

quiz.prompt: What caused the Port Harcourt inventory system to feel unfinished after delivery?

options.text: The team stopped at delivery and skipped training, handover and closing the business side

quiz.explanation: Closing includes handover, training, final payments and records. Delivery alone is not closure.

quiz.prompt: What is the best first rule for choosing a project tool?

options.text: Pick the one with the most features
Choose the one a famous company uses
Choose the one your team will actually open and use

quiz.explanation: A tool nobody uses fails. Prefer simple, check phone and offline use, and keep data exportable.

quiz.prompt: Why should you check a tool's current pricing page instead of trusting an old article?

options.text: Features, free limits and prices change often

quiz.explanation: The lesson says to check the current free plan before you rely on a tool, including anything you read in the course.

quiz.prompt: What does the lesson say about this course and PMI certification hours?

options.text: It counts toward the PMI training hours
It is not PMI-authorised training and does not count toward the required hours

quiz.explanation: The course teaches ideas that certifications test, but certification courses, exams and fees are separate.

quiz.prompt: As checked in the lesson, which CAPM requirement is stated by PMI?

options.text: At least 23 hours of project management education before the exam and no experience requirement

quiz.explanation: Requirements can change, so read PMI's current page before you plan.

quiz.prompt: Which is a realistic way to start gaining project experience, according to the lesson?

options.text: Volunteer to organise a real event or change in your job or study and document it
Claim experience you do not have
Wait for a certificate before doing any project

quiz.explanation: Real, documented projects build evidence of your skill and make your work visible.

quiz.prompt: Which is the best choice for a capstone project?

options.text: A real project small enough to plan in a few days that matters to you
A project entirely outside your control

quiz.explanation: Too vague, too large or out of your control makes planning hard. Real stakes teach more.

quiz.prompt: In the specimen plan, a contingency of ₦70,000 on a subtotal of ₦380,000 is about:
quiz.explanation: 70,000 / 380,000 is about 0.184, so about 18 percent, justified by permit and weather uncertainty.

quiz.prompt: What should a five-minute briefing end with?

options.text: A specific request, such as an approval, money, people or a decision

quiz.explanation: A briefing without a request is just a talk.

quiz.prompt: Which rubric point checks that your plan can stand on its own?

options.text: The plan is longer than ten pages
Another person could pick it up and run the project without asking you what you meant

quiz.explanation: A good plan is clear enough for someone else to run, honest about uncertainty and tested with real people and numbers.

quiz.prompt: What should you do with every number in your plan?

options.text: Make sure it is real, sourced or clearly marked as an estimate or assumption

quiz.explanation: Honest plans label uncertainty. A precise-looking number with no source misleads.

flashcards.back: Temporary work that creates a unique product, service or result. It has a start and an end.
Work that repeats the same process again and again, aiming for reliability and efficiency.
Scope, time, cost and quality. They are linked, so changing one moves at least one other.
Delivery success means finishing within agreed limits. Result success means what you made actually solves the problem.
Show the effect of a request on scope, time and cost and let the decision-maker choose.
Initiate, plan, execute, monitor and control (alongside), close.
Plan most of the work up front, then execute and manage change formally. Best when requirements are clear and change is costly.
Plan in short cycles, deliver usable pieces, get feedback and adapt. Best when requirements are unclear and change is cheap.
Use predictive and agile methods in different parts of the same project, where each fits.
How clear is the result? What does change cost? Can I get frequent feedback? Do contracts demand fixed scope, price or date?
Specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound (a common modern version). Credited to George T. Doran, 1981, whose original words differed.
A description of what is in scope, what is out of scope, and what is not yet decided.
The tests the result must pass before the sponsor accepts it, covering both delivery and result.
A short document that formally starts the project: purpose, goal, scope, key dates, budget, people, assumptions, constraints, first risks.
An assumption is treated as true without proof. A constraint is a limit you cannot change.
Anyone who can affect your project or be affected by it.
Sorts stakeholders into manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed and monitor.
High power, lower interest: give short updates and never surprise them.
A table of who needs what information, how often, through which channel and from whom.
A tree that breaks the project scope into deliverables, down to work packages.
The lowest level of the WBS: small enough to estimate, own and mark done or not done.
The pieces under a parent must add up to the whole parent, with nothing missing and nothing extra.
Could two people agree whether it is finished? Can one person be responsible for it?
A rule of thumb for work package size. A guide, not a law.
The habit of predicting tasks will take less time than they do, by imagining the smooth path.
(O + 4M + P) / 6, with O optimistic, M most likely and P pessimistic.
(P - O) / 6, a rough measure of uncertainty.
Effort is work hours, duration is calendar time, waiting time is when nothing happens.
Visible time or money added at project level for uncertainty, owned by the manager.
Adding people to a late software project tends to make it later.
B cannot start until A finishes. The most common kind of dependency.
The longest chain of dependent activities. It sets the earliest finish date and has zero float.
How long an activity can slip without delaying the project.
Crashing adds resources to critical activities. Fast tracking runs activities in parallel that were in sequence.
A forced wait between activities, such as concrete curing.
Price each work package, then add up the results.
Fixed costs stay the same with quantity. Variable costs rise with quantity.
Contingency is for expected risks and the manager controls it. Management reserve is held by the sponsor for the unforeseen.

flashcards.front: Fixed price, time and materials, cost plus
flashcards.back: Three payment types that put the risk of cost overrun on different parties.
Add each person's assigned hours by week. If it exceeds real availability, the plan is broken.
A risk is an uncertain event that might happen. An issue has already happened or is certain.
Probability x impact in money.
Avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept.
Imagine the project has already failed and write down why, to find risks early.
A table of risks with likelihood, impact, response, trigger and owner, reviewed regularly.
Forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning.
Team members feel safe to take risks, ask questions, admit mistakes and disagree. First of Google's five factors in Project Aristotle.
Responsible does it, Accountable owns the result (only one), Consulted gives input, Informed is told.
State the outcome, give authority with responsibility, agree check-ins and match control to the person.
A fixed-length event of one month or less with a Sprint Goal. The next begins as soon as one ends.
Product Owner, Developers and Scrum Master.
The Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum (15 minutes), Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective.
A cap on work in progress in a Kanban stage, forcing finishing before starting.
Average time to finish = work in progress / throughput.
A line that names the decision needed, not just a topic.
End a meeting by reading actions, owners and dates aloud.
Green on track, amber at risk with a plan, red off track and help needed.
A simple record of date, decision, who made it and why.
The saved, agreed plan used to measure progress. Changed only by formal decision.
Planned value, earned value and actual cost.
SV = EV - PV. CV = EV - AC. SPI = EV / PV. CPI = EV / AC. EAC = BAC / CPI.
The slow growth of a project through small unapproved additions.
Capture, assess, decide, update, communicate.
A position is what someone says they want. An interest is why they want it.
Separate people from the problem, focus on interests, invent options, use objective criteria. From Fisher and Ury, 1981.
Best alternative to a negotiated agreement.
Competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating.
When it is outside your authority, you are stuck after reasonable steps, or it threatens the critical path, safety, law or the client.
Assurance builds quality into the process. Control inspects and tests the result.
The agreement, recorded in writing, that the result meets the agreed criteria.
Giving the users what they need to use and maintain the result: instructions, training, contacts, access.
What went well? What went badly? Why? What will we do differently next time?
A planned review some time after handover to confirm the project achieved its purpose.
Pick what the team will actually use, keep it simple, check phone and offline use, keep data exportable.
A reusable set of documents: charter, stakeholders, WBS, schedule, budget, risk register, RACI, status update, change log, lessons learned.
PMI's entry-level certification. Check the current requirements on PMI's page before applying.
This course is not PMI-authorised training and does not count toward certification hours.
Charter, method, stakeholders, WBS, estimates, schedule, budget and people, risks, team and control, close.
Problem and goal, in and out of scope, the one-page plan, top risks, the ask, questions.
Another person could pick up the plan and run the project without asking you what you meant.

# Sources and credits

Everything in this course is written in original words. Ideas are credited here so you can read the originals. All people, companies, places, prices and numbers in worked examples are invented for practice unless a source is named. Sources were checked on 23 and 24 October 2026 by the course writer, and a second pass was made on 24 October 2026 by a separate reviewer (an AI agent, not a human expert). Prices, tool limits and certification rules change, so check the current official pages before you rely on them.

## Checked against a named source

- **Agile Manifesto, "Manifesto for Agile Software Development" (2001).** The four value pairs and the sentence "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more" were checked against the signatories page on agilemanifesto.org. https://agilemanifesto.org/display/000000365.html
- **Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland, *The Scrum Guide* (2020).** Sprint length of one month or less, the three accountabilities, five events, three artifacts with their commitments, the 15-minute Daily Scrum, and the maximum timeboxes for Sprint Planning (eight hours) and the Retrospective (three hours) for a one-month Sprint. https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html
- **Bruce W. Tuckman, "Developmental sequence in small groups," *Psychological Bulletin*, 63, 384 to 399 (1965).** Four stages. Tuckman's own 1984 commentary on the paper confirms the stages and the 1977 addition of "adjourning" (Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen, "Stages of small-group development revisited," *Group and Organization Studies*, 1977). https://garfield.library.upenn.edu/classics1984/A1984TD25600001.pdf
- **Roger Buehler, Dale Griffin and Michael Ross, "Exploring the planning fallacy," *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* (1994).** The thesis-student figures used in Lesson 6 (about 34 days predicted, about 55 days actual, about 30 percent finishing within the predicted time, worst-case average about 49 days with about half finishing by then). https://bear.warrington.ufl.edu/brenner/mar7588/Papers/buehler-et-al-1994.pdf
- **Bent Flyvbjerg, database of about 16,000 projects; "only 8.5 percent" meet initial cost and time estimates.** Checked against a published interview summary at the IT University of Copenhagen. Flyvbjerg's book is *How Big Things Get Done* (2023, with Dan Gardner). The reference class forecasting idea was checked against PMI's summary. https://pure.itu.dk/en/clippings/why-big-projects-go-wrong/ and https://www.pmi.org/learning/library/nobel-project-management-reference-class-forecasting-8068
- **Google re:Work, "Understand team effectiveness" (Project Aristotle).** The five dynamics in order of importance: psychological safety, dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, impact. The page says it was originally published in 2015. https://rework.withgoogle.com/intl/en/guides/understand-team-effectiveness
- **PMI, "What is a project."** The definition of a project as a temporary endeavour to create a unique product, service or result. https://www.pmi.org/about/what-is-a-project
- **PMI certification pages (checked 24 October 2026).** CAPM eligibility (secondary education, age 18, 23 hours of project management education, no experience) and the July 2026 PMP update (domain weighting change, 35 hours of training, live training provider rule from late Q4 2026). https://www.pmi.org/certifications/certified-associate-capm and https://www.pmi.org/certifications/project-management-pmp/new-exam
- **PERT history and the three-point formula.** PERT was developed in the late 1950s for the US Navy Polaris programme. The formulas expected time = (O + 4M + P) / 6 and standard deviation = (P - O) / 6 are the standard PERT beta approximations, taught in PMI learning material. https://www.pmi.org/learning/library/leveraging-new-practice-standard-project-estimating-6222
- **Earned value formulas** (PV, EV, AC, SV, CV, SPI, CPI, EAC = BAC / CPI) checked against US Department of Energy earned value guidance, and the arithmetic in Lesson 13 was recomputed by hand.
- **PRINCE2 7** principles, including continued business justification and learning from experience, checked against the publisher's summary of the seven principles.
- **Gantt charts.** Henry Gantt's charts from the early 1900s. Karol Adamiecki devised a similar harmonogram in 1896 but published mostly in Polish and Russian. Checked against encyclopaedic summaries and by the independent reviewer.
- **Daniel Vacanti and Yuval Yeret, *The Kanban Guide* (2020).** Three core practices (defining and visualising a workflow, actively managing items, improving the workflow) and the flow measures (cycle time, throughput, work item age, work in progress). Checked by the independent reviewer against the published guide. https://kanbanguides.org/the-kanban-guide/2020.12
